papers.selection_reason: Introduces asymmetric sparse attention with decoupled key/value heads for faster LLM decoding, an architectural and efficiency contribution.
papers.title: More Value per Key: Asymmetric Sparse Attention for Faster LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: SAGA accelerates long-context LLM decoding by using fewer key heads than value heads, while preserving quality with sparse attention.

papers.abstract: Beyond scaling their parameters and data, large language models currently gain versatility on new problems along a single axis: the tokens they spend on chain-of-thought (CoT). We investigate whether dynamic routing programs, which execute a subset of the model's layers or iterate some of them, can open a second axis of test-time adaptation, complementary to CoT and free of any gradient update. Prior work showed that such programs exist and bring accuracy and efficiency gains on problems similar to those they were trained on; we ask whether they can also be identified rapidly, from a handful of demonstrations (3 or 10), by a strategy that transfers across models and tasks without training. First, we find that strategies that select programs by the probability they assign to the demonstrations' labels, arbitrated by the model's own confidence, bring consistent gains: on average over the 49 tasks of MMLU and substantially on four of seven models, and most of all on far out-of-distribution tasks such as ARC-AGI, where programs double the accuracy of a 7B model whose CoT fails. Second, on MMLU across the seven post-trained models, routing complements CoT in practice: the two succeed on different queries, and their composition exceeds CoT alone. Despite these gains, our analyses show that confidence-based selection leaves much of the potential untapped, in two places in particular: (1) in surfacing the routing potential that is already present early in pre-training but becomes harder to select after post-training, and (2) in making models robust to the refinements routing introduces, since unsuccessful routes tend to drive the residual stream out of the distribution that the following layers expect. Together, our results point to dynamic routing as a paradigm for extending the plasticity of existing and future LLMs in rapid test-time adaptation.
authors: Michal \v{S}tef\'anik, Marek Kadl\v{c}\'ik, Josef Kucha\v{r}, Michal Spiegel
bullets: Selects routing programs from only 3 or 10 demonstrations using label likelihood and the model’s confidence, without gradient updates or task-specific training.
Produces consistent gains across 49 MMLU tasks and seven models, with especially large benefits on far-out-of-distribution ARC-AGI tasks.
Routing and chain-of-thought succeed on different queries; combining them outperforms chain-of-thought alone on MMLU.
Selection remains limited: post-training can obscure routing potential, and unsuccessful routes may push representations outside the distribution expected by later layers.
Scope: results focus on rapid, confidence-based program selection across benchmark tasks and models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Programs of layers for a 12-layer model. Boxes are layer applications in execution order; blue boxes re-apply a contiguous block (a cycle), the dashed box is a skipped layer. Every program runs the unchanged pretrained weights and is read out in one forward pass.

Figure 3: Decision-point design of §5.2: minimal pairs on both sides. (a) Programs that differ only in one extra pass over a block, graded helpful or harmful by the flip of the answer. papers.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.
authors: Sribalaji C. Anand, George J. Pappas
bullets: Studies stealthy insider attacks in multi-robot LLM teams performing physically verifiable surveys.
Derives a lower bound on how often adversarial reports are verified using communication-graph degrees and verification budget.
Bounds worst-case map error via a linear program over adversarial bias distributions.
Finds a tradeoff: rare, full-scale lies are optimal below a critical verification level, while small noise-hidden biases are preferable above it.
LLM-agent experiments support both bounds; re-check choices appear unbiased, but re-check magnitudes are unpredictable.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates stealthy insider attacks on LLM-based robot teams, analyzing the interaction between LLM agents and verification budgets in a grounded task.
papers.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
papers.tldr: A single compromised LLM-controlled robot can stealthily distort a robot team’s survey map by exploiting limited verification budgets, with attack strategies changing sharply at a critical verification level.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.
authors: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye, Junxuan Shen, Cheng Zhu, Aurora Ruggeri, Kelvin Cheung, Jiayuan Mao, Edward Adelson, Jiajun Wu, Robert D. Howe, Yilun Du
bullets: Replaces specialized force/tactile sensing with visual force prediction from a compliant gripper’s deformation.
Trains a visual force estimator to annotate demonstrations with estimated forces.
Learns an action–force proposal policy that generates candidate actions and predicted forces.
At test time, selects the action whose predicted force best matches a target force from demonstrations.
Evaluated on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of visual force estimation and inference-time force search. (b) During inference-time force search, the policy jointly samples candidate end-effector actions and force values. We execute the action from the sample whose generated force value most closely matches the target force.

Fig. 7. Representative successful rollouts of four force-sensitive manipulation tasks using force-based candidate selection. Each row shows a task sequence progressing from left to right. For empty soda can grasping and berry picking, the robot applies sufficient gripping force to lift and transfer the object without crushing it. During plug insertion, the robot maintains sufficient contact friction to prevent slippage and fully inserts the plug into the socket.

papers.abstract: A pedestrian with a phone could be shown where nearby people will be in the next few seconds, if the forecast stays on the ground while the phone moves, is calibrated, and needs only a monocular camera and visual-inertial odometry (VIO). We build and evaluate such a system. People are detected, lifted onto the floor by ray-plane intersection, tracked in a gravity-aligned metric frame, and forecast as per-step probability maps by a small U-Net trained with a negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss on bird's-eye (SDD) and first-person (EgoTraj-Bench) trajectories. On handheld ADVIO recordings, vertical VIO drift and the user's own changes of level silently rescale monocular ground positions (by 87% within 90 s on one clip; on another, all tracks are lost for the last 31% of the clip); keeping the camera's height above the floor constant under a low-pass-filtered altitude avoids this, though it lags on escalators. On the SDD and EgoTraj-Bench test splits, the final forecaster lowers the NLL at 4.8 s by 1.51 and 1.37 nats relative to a fitted constant-velocity Gaussian. Lacking ground truth for people in handheld video, we score forecasts against the tracker's own later raw measurements. In an internally pre-registered evaluation on seven held-out clips, the final forecaster's NLL is lower than the benchmark-fitted baseline's at 1.2, 2.4 and 4.8 s (by 0.17, 0.23 and 0.47 nats; 95% intervals over people exclude zero), but by less than half as much as on the development clips. Exploratory analyses cut both ways: resampling clips instead of people widens the intervals to include zero at 1.2 and 2.4 s, and once both forecasters are recalibrated on the development clips the network is significantly better only at 1.2 s; but two clips run with ADVIO's reference poses favour the network much more when re-run with the phone's own poses. We discuss what such self-consistency scores can and cannot show.
authors: Danial Safaei
bullets: Detects people, projects them onto the floor, tracks them in a metric frame, and predicts per-step probability heat maps with a small U-Net.
A low-pass-filtered fixed camera-height constraint reduces severe monocular VIO height drift, though it lags during escalator motion.
On SDD and EgoTraj-Bench, the forecaster improves 4.8-second NLL over a constant-velocity Gaussian baseline.
On seven held-out handheld clips, it achieves lower self-consistency NLL at 1.2, 2.4, and 4.8 seconds, with smaller gains than on development clips.
Evaluation uses trackers’ later raw measurements rather than ground-truth pedestrian positions; results vary with resampling, recalibration, and pose source.

papers.title: Probabilistic Pedestrian Forecasts from a Handheld Phone: World-Frame Heat Maps, Visual-Inertial Height Drift, and Evaluation without Ground Truth

papers.abstract: In worker-equipment proximity monitoring, video transformers are widely used for collision anticipation and have demonstrated strong performance. However, their accuracy comes with substantial computational demands, creating a tension with the need for low-latency inference on mobile robots and the pursuit of lower-carbon computation in construction. To address this, this study investigates where computation within an established video transformer is redundant and whether that redundancy can be removed without materially degrading predictive performance. Using VideoMAEv2-Base on the Nexar Collision Prediction dataset, we first examine how collision-relevant information evolves across network depth and then investigate two complementary forms of redundancy: structured capacity redundancy in multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and spatiotemporal redundancy in the token stream. Linear probes show that interpretable motion cues, including flow magnitude, looming, and approach versus retreat, are most accessible at intermediate layers, whereas collision-label discrimination strengthens toward the final layer. Token redundancy is axis-specific: adjacent temporal-token similarity reaches 0.970 in later layers, while spatial similarity falls to 0.297, indicating substantially greater redundancy across time than across space. Exploiting this asymmetry, temporal token merging reduces backbone computation from 356.99 to 178.50 GFLOPs and latency from 12.69 to 7.21 ms per clip, a 1.76x speedup, while mean average precision changes only from 0.7478 to 0.7443. Importance-guided retention of 50% of MLP units preserves an AUC of 0.753, compared with 0.529 under matched random retention, and reveals that pruning alters score calibration before discriminative ranking collapses. These findings establish a new pathway for pursuing faster algorithms through targeted temporal token compression and neuron pruning.
authors: Xiaoshan Zhou
bullets: Intermediate layers expose motion cues, while collision discrimination becomes strongest near the final layer.
Later-layer tokens are far more redundant across time than across space, motivating temporal rather than spatial compression.
Merging temporal tokens cuts backbone computation roughly in half and yields a 1.76× speedup, with only a small mAP change.
Importance-guided retention of 50% of MLP units preserves AUC much better than matched random retention.
The results support targeted temporal token compression and neuron pruning for lower-latency, lower-carbon mobile-robot inference.

(D) Expected calibration error before and after validation-only sigmoid scaling. (E) Balanced accuracy at fixed and validation-selected thresholds. Error bars for random retention summarize three seeds. Unit-retention ratios differ from estimated whole-model parameter fractions.

papers.abstract: Structural diagrams are widely used to represent complex systems and relational information across scientific, engineering, procedural, and spatial domains. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have become increasingly capable of recognizing diagram elements and reasoning about their content, while complete diagram topology extraction remains comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we study diagram-to-graph topology extraction: extracting all diagram entities and the complete relations among them. To enable large-scale supervised training and systematic evaluation of this task, we introduce Knossos, a benchmark of 19,200 diagrams across six diverse domains, with 245,179 nodes and 439,740 edges. Its symbolic generation process provides exact alignment between rendered diagrams and annotations of complete topology, relation types, and connector geometry. To address the modeling challenge of complete topology extraction, we also present Ariadne, a structured framework that decomposes the task into node inventory extraction and source-conditioned edge prediction. Extensive experiments show that training on Knossos substantially improves complete topology extraction in smaller open-source VLMs. Ariadne further improves over one-step extraction under matched supervision, demonstrating the additional benefit of structured decomposition. It achieves the highest average Edge F1 among the evaluated methods on Knossos, while both backbone variants also improve over their unadapted counterparts on the real-world external benchmark. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/bangwayne/knossos_Ariadne_Public.
authors: Bangwei Guo, Xujiang Zhao, Shengyu Chen, Yanchi Liu, Wei Cheng, Xi Zhu, Guoning Zhang, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Haifeng Chen
bullets: Introduces Knossos, a 19,200-diagram benchmark spanning six domains with complete topology, relation types, and connector-geometry annotations.
Uses symbolic generation to provide exact alignment between diagrams and graph annotations for supervised training and evaluation.
Presents Ariadne, which separates node inventory extraction from source-conditioned edge prediction.
Training on Knossos improves smaller open-source VLMs; Ariadne outperforms one-step extraction under matched supervision.
Both evaluated backbone variants also improve on an external real-world benchmark, though the scope of results is tied to the evaluated methods and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: In a Transformer, token mixing is the step that lets each token draw information from other tokens, and it dominates the cost of encoding long sequences. Self-attention does this mixing very well: every token weighs every other token by content, which gives strong contextual modeling. That all-pairs comparison is also why its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. We introduce WNet, a Transformer encoder that replaces self-attention with token mixing based on the discrete wavelet transform (DWT). Three attention-free mixers recombine the scales: by linear fusion, by learned gating, or by letting each token choose its scales. A hybrid adds self-attention in the last layer only. A receptive-field analysis shows that wavelet mixers built from two-tap filters, such as Haar, never relate tokens outside fixed blocks, however deep the network, even when the filters are learned. Longer filters reach the whole sequence within two layers. We pre-train every model with masked language modeling on a fixed-token subset of C4 and fine-tune on GLUE, using one controlled setup with size-matched BERT and FNet baselines and a control that cannot mix tokens. The token-gated mixer trains as fast as attention at 256 tokens and 2.7 times faster at 4,096.
authors: Rana Aref Salama, Abdou Youssef, Mona Diab
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of all-pairs self-attention for long sequences.
Uses discrete wavelet transforms with linear fusion, learned gating, or token-specific scale selection.
A hybrid variant adds self-attention only in the final layer.
Two-tap filters have fixed-block receptive fields; longer filters can cover the full sequence within two layers.
The token-gated mixer trains as fast as attention at 256 tokens and 2.7× faster at 4,096 tokens in the reported setup.

papers.abstract: Memory is essential for long-horizon robotic manipulation, where successful actions may depend on past events that are no longer recoverable from the current observation. As episodes grow longer, however, retaining the full history becomes increasingly costly, creating a fundamental scalability challenge for memory-augmented policies. Existing approaches address this challenge by either storing selected past observations in a bounded memory bank or compressing interaction history into a fixed-size parametric state through Test-Time Training (TTT). Yet these formulations do not explicitly distinguish between historical information that can already be recovered from the policy's current context and information that must persist beyond it. We introduce TTT-RM, which repurposes TTT as Residual Memory, using fast weights not to generically compress history but to complement a bounded memory bank by preserving task-relevant historical information that cannot be recovered from the policy's current context. Concretely, TTT-RM learns a history decoder that reconstructs historical representations from the current observation and retrieved memory. The resulting reconstruction residual captures what this context fails to explain and serves as the learning target for TTT. The TTT slow weights are optimized against this residual target so that online fast-weight updates learn to encode complementary historical information over time. The fast-weight state is then queried to produce a residual memory representation that conditions action generation. Extensive experiments on memory-intensive simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show that TTT-RM consistently improves across multiple memory designs, outperforms diverse baselines, and supports sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.
authors: Haoxuan Wang, Gengyu Zhang, Ramana Rao Kompella, Gaowen Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of remembering task-relevant events during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses a bounded memory bank plus a history decoder to identify unrecoverable information as a reconstruction residual.
Trains Test-Time Training fast weights online to encode this residual and conditions action generation on the resulting representation.
Experiments across simulation and real-world tasks show consistent improvements across memory designs and baselines.
Demonstrates sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Real-world results. Qualitative rollouts across the three manipulation tasks are paired with quantitative task progress profiles, which report the fraction of trials reaching or exceeding each progress threshold. Our method consistently achieves better performance across all task stages.

Figure 3: Ablation studies. (a) shows the effect of the residual-loss weight λres. Disabling residual supervision (λres = 0) can degrade performance, while moderate values yield the strongest results. (b) compares TTT-RM with a naive EM+TTT combination, showing that simply adding TTT to an EM-equipped policy provides limited benefit. (c) examines the effect of our three-stage training pipeline, with the full procedure achieving the best performance across both EM variants.

Figure 2: Overview of TTT-RM. Frozen visual features are selectively stored in Explicit Memory and written into TTT fast weights through the visual-stream writer. During training, the history decoder estimates what past information is recoverable from the existing policy context, and its reconstruction residual supervises Residual Memory. At inference, the decoder is removed, while Explicit Memory and Residual Memory jointly condition action generation.

Figure 1: Comparison of memory paradigms. Incoming observations are represented as tokens along the timeline. (a) Explicit Memory retains selected historical information in a bounded memory bank, giving direct access to only a sparse subset of the preceding history. (b) Test-Time Training instead compresses history into a fixed-size fast-weight state whose size does not grow with episode length. (c) TTT as Residual Memory. TTT is repurposed to preserve only the historical information not recoverable from the current observation and retrieved memory.

papers.selection_reason: Repurposes Test-Time Training as Residual Memory to preserve task-relevant historical information for long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Test-Time Training as Residual Memory for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: TTT-RM augments bounded robot-policy memory with test-time-trained fast weights that retain only historical information missing from the current context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for online reinforcement learning (RL), enabling multimodal behaviors and improved performance. However, training these policies remains challenging: the critic specifies the desired policy as an unnormalized Boltzmann density but does not provide direct samples from it. Many existing methods rely on importance sampling to construct training signals, which can suffer from high variance, increasing computational cost and destabilizing training. We propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for training generative models to sample from unnormalized densities without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. We learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing target posterior mean estimation. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions, first for the terminal density and then for the trainable velocity field. We prove that their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that conditional flow matching (CFM) would recover if target samples were available. We formulate the velocity condition as a fixed-point equation and exploit its conditional-expectation structure to construct a stop-gradient objective for enforcing it. The resulting training procedure retains the scalable sample-interpolate-regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, using endpoints generated by the current flow. For online RL, the critic gradient supplies the target score at the generated actions, yielding a direct approach to actor training. Experiments on RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, while substantially reducing training time.
authors: Zeyang Li, Yunan Wang, Risheek Garrepalli, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Navid Azizan
bullets: Addresses high-variance importance sampling when training diffusion or flow policies from unnormalized Boltzmann targets.
Uses target scores and flow-matching self-consistency to learn the desired terminal density and velocity field without target samples.
Implements a stop-gradient fixed-point objective with the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of conditional flow matching.
In online RL, critic gradients provide the target score for direct actor training.
Experiments on RL benchmarks report competitive or improved performance over generative-policy baselines with substantially lower training time.

papers.title: Score-Calibrated Flow for Sampling from Unnormalized Densities with Applications to Generative Online Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Activation steering has proven effective for controlling the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) at inference time, but its application to SpeechLLMs remains new, and training-free steering approaches for such models are still largely unexplored. We propose a training-free Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) protocol that derives steering vectors for common speech tasks (e.g. transcription) in SpeechLLMs from a small number of labeled utterances. We showcase that adding these vectors in the representation space, at inference time, enforces better the targeted speech task. We further show that, when combined with prompting, these vectors yield to consistent improvement over prompting alone on most evaluated tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) or Emotion Recognition (ER), and transfer to out-of-domain data. We additionally demonstrate the usefulness of script-normalization directions to enforce the target script of a specific language.
authors: S\'everin Baroudi, Yanis Labrak, Pierfrancesco Melucci, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek, Herv\'e Bredin, Mirco Ravanelli, Ricard Marxer
bullets: Addresses the limited exploration of training-free activation steering for SpeechLLMs.
Derives steering vectors from a small number of labeled utterances using Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA).
Applies vectors in representation space during inference to reinforce tasks such as transcription and emotion recognition.
Combining steering with prompting consistently improves most evaluated tasks over prompting alone and transfers to out-of-domain data.
Also introduces script-normalization directions to enforce a target script for a given language.

papers.title: Steering Speech-Language Models: Training-Free Task Specialization via Contrastive Activation Addition

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen $\pi 0.5$ policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4% to 66.2%, outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time. We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same $\pi 0.5$ policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4% to 55.4%. These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/.
authors: Jiuzhou Lei, Chang Liu, Dayou Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xiao Liang, Yu She, Zhiwen Fan, Minghui Zheng
bullets: Targets degraded performance on out-of-distribution task variations while preserving existing policy capabilities.
Trains linear classifiers on successful and failed rollouts to identify outcome-relevant intervention locations and task-specific steering directions.
On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen π0.5 policy, raises average success from 44.4% to 66.2% with little added inference time.
Also improves real-robot manipulation and Cosmos Policy performance, raising Cosmos Policy’s average success from 35.4% to 55.4%.
Scope: evaluated on simulated and real-robot manipulation with π0.5 and on a world-action model; policy parameters remain frozen.

papers.tldr: RoboIRS improves out-of-distribution robot-policy performance at inference time by steering internal representations using successful and failed rollouts, without updating policy parameters.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on new text degrades what it already does. Replay-free projectors such as Adam-NSCL and GPM forbid one shared subspace of a layer's inputs in every row of the update. The tropical geometry of a ReLU layer shows why this is too coarse. In data space, the units' walls are tropical hypersurfaces whose cells are dual to the upper vertices of a zonotope; in weight space, each old token is a hyperplane, and the tokens cut out a polyhedron, the closure of the weights that keep every token on its side. An exact identity joins the two pictures: the squared change of the layer's output under any weight change splits into in-cell, open-to-closed and closed-to-open terms, and the first two live on the tokens each unit fires on. The identity names a gate-aware per-unit projector, and a budget-separation theorem prices exact protection: it costs a unit the rank of its own open tokens, while a shared subspace pays at least the rank of their union in every row. On OPT-1.3b, where 96% of (token, unit) pairs are closed, the projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL at all six matched budgets from 9 to 60 constrained directions per row, the gap widening from $1.1\times$ to $4.3\times$; with 1/5.5 of the directions it halves the forgetting of Adam-NSCL at GPM's energy threshold. On OPT-6.7b, it matches Adam-NSCL's forgetting at matched budget while learning more. As the theory predicts, the open/closed partition is the operative variable: open tokens beat random, sign-blind and anti-gate token sets on 18 of 18 seed-pairs. In pruning repair, every derivative-based local model of the output error at the dense weights is blind to pairs that open: the minimisers of the gate-weighted objective can leave the polyhedron, the objective's closed-form solution is 1.94 nats worse than no repair on OPT-1.3b, and a convex one-sided penalty bounds the escape.
authors: Yuyang Zhang, Xiaoyin Chen, Chunlin Ren, Qihuang Zhang
bullets: Shared projectors protect one common input subspace across all rows, while ReLU geometry motivates protecting each unit’s own open-token subspace.
An exact output-change decomposition identifies the tokens relevant to each unit and yields a per-unit projector.
A budget-separation theorem shows that per-unit protection can require fewer constrained directions than protecting the union of tokens across rows.
On OPT-1.3b, the projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL across six matched budgets, with the gap increasing from 1.1× to 4.3×; on OPT-6.7b, it matches forgetting while learning more.

The open/closed gate partition is central: open-token choices outperform random, sign-blind, and anti-gate choices in all reported seed-pair comparisons; a convex one-sided penalty limits gate escape during pruning repair.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A layer’s weights, its lifted Newton polytope, and its activation pattern, for a toy layer of three ReLU units on two inputs. Pale blue marks weight space and (c), (d) are data space; arrows marked dual join the two. (a) Each colour is a unit and each vertex a set of units that fire, in bits (101: units 1 and 3), placed at their summed weights and raised by their summed biases: the Newton polytope of ∑ i max(0, zi) lifted by the biases (Zhang et al., 2018) (Appendix A). (b) Its shadow, which subdivides the Newton polytope; the circled vertex is unit 1’s weights w. (c) The units’ walls zi = 0 in data space. Regions are labelled by which units fire, each is a vertex of (b), and pattern 110 (hollow in (a)) occurs nowhere. (d) Fine-tuning moves unit 1’s wall from w to ŵ, and colours say what that does to each old token: green stays open, blue closes, red opens, grey stays closed (the sets S++, S+−, S−+, S−− of Theorem 5). (e) The same move in weight space: w is a point and each old token a line, crossing which flips the token (dark: open at w; light: closed; D’s line is off-panel). The grey region PX is the closure of the weights that flip no token (Definition 3). (f) Our projector (§3) fixes the pre-activation on the open tokens A and C, so w moves only parallel to their lines (dotted) and the closed token E may open; circles are the new-task loss. Each row is one unit, that is one row of the layer’s first weight matrix (fc1 in OPT), and each column is one old token, so the cell in row i and column t is the pair (t, i). Only 38 of the 240 pairs, 16%, are open; at OPT-1.3b the share is 4%. (b)–(d) A cell’s shade is the fraction of an isotropic weight update’s effect on that pair’s pre-activation that the constraint removes: white means the pair is left free, and full colour means it is held exactly. The dots repeat the open pairs of (a). The bar to the right of a row is the number of directions the constraint forbids in that row, and the dashed line marks the mean, which is 3 for every family. The bar under a grid is the mean shade over the open pairs. Holding a closed pair guards only against its opening. (b) The shared subspace of Adam-NSCL, GPM, InfLoRA and AlphaEdit forbids the top 3 eigendirections of the old inputs’ second moment, and it forbids them in every row. Every row therefore spends 3 directions, and a cell’s shade depends only on its column: the leftmost token is held at 83% in every row and the rightmost at 8%. The top unit’s 8 open tokens are held at between 9% and 78%. Overall 56% of the open pairs’ effect is held. (c) Methods that protect whole units freeze entire rows; HAT and AGS-CL choose them by old-task use, and MIGU by new-data magnitude. A frozen row spends all 30 of its directions (arrow), so a mean of 3 buys one frozen row out of ten. The top row is frozen. All 24 of its tokens are held, including the 16 on which it is closed, and no other row holds anything, so 21% of the open pairs’ effect is held. (d) Our projector gives unit i the budget ki = min(C,#open) with cap C = 4, and spends it on that unit’s own open tokens with the largest activations. The top unit therefore holds its 4 most active open tokens exactly, and its other 4 open tokens only in part, at 54%, 22%, 14% and 10%. A unit with 3 open tokens holds all 3 exactly, and the bottom unit, which never fires, receives ki = 0 and holds nothing. The budgets, top to bottom, are 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 1, 0, which also average 3, and 85% of the open pairs’ effect is held. (e) The selector controls of §4.2, drawn for the top unit. Its 24 old tokens are sorted by pre-activation z, shown by the bars with the open tokens on the left, and the dotted line is the wall. Eight are open, and its budget is ki = 4. Each row marks the 4 tokens that one selector spends the budget on. The gate takes the 4 most active open tokens. Random-within-open takes 4 of the 8 open tokens at random, here sharing one with the gate. The first-order criterion takes the 4 tokens with the largest |∂L/∂z|; since that derivative is zero on closed tokens, it also stays inside the open set. Random tokens draws 4 of all 24, and here lands on 1 open and 3 closed tokens. The sign-blind criterion takes the 4 largest |z− θ|, which are the 2 most open and the 2 most deeply closed tokens, and the anti-gate takes the 4 most deeply closed. Four objectives are compared, as in the legend: the pre-activation error ∑ x(ẑ−z)2, which SparseGPT and GPTQ fit; the Gauss–Newton and Fisher models of the post-activation error, which reduce to the in-cell error on the open tokens, Lgated (Lemma 13); the exact post-activation error Lpost; and ours, Lgated h, which adds to that in-cell error a penalty of weight λ on closed tokens that open, the one-sided penalty of Theorem 15. (a) The price each objective charges one token that is open at w, here with z = 1, as its new pre-activation ẑ moves; shading marks the open side of the wall. The pre-activation, curvature and our objectives charge the same parabola (ẑ − z)2, drawn as three coincident curves. The exact error agrees with them while the token stays open, and stops growing once it closes. A move to ẑ = −1 costs 4 under the three quadratics but only 1 under the exact error, because the unit’s output cannot fall below 0. (b) The same for a token closed at w, here with z = −1. The pre-activation objective still charges (ẑ − z)2, so a move to ẑ = −2, deeper into the closed side and with no effect on the output, costs 1. The curvature models charge nothing anywhere, even after the token opens. The exact error charges only opening, max(ẑ, 0)2, and ours charges λ times that, with λ = 3 here. A move to ẑ = 1 thus costs 4 under pre-activation, 0 under curvature, 1 under the exact error and 3 under ours. (c) What each objective does to a pruned row. Take unit 1 of Figure 1, with w = (1, 0.4), old tokens A and C open and E and D closed. Prune w1,1 to 0 and let each objective refit w1,2 alone. The horizontal axis is the refitted w1,2, and the curve is the exact error along it (log scale). The dotted lines mark where E opens (w1,2 = 0.50) and where A and C open again (1.65 and 2.85). No point of this line keeps every gate: A and C need w1,2 > 2.85, while E needs w1,2 ≤ 0.50. In this toy no refit therefore improves on leaving the pruned row alone at w1,2 = 0.4, where A, C and E are all closed and the exact error is 2.45; the objectives differ in how much they lose. The curvature fit sees only A and C and restores both exactly, by moving to w1,2 = 4.13. That opens E to zE = 7.26, and the exact error there is 52.8, 22× that of no repair. The pre-activation fit, at 0.81, keeps A and C closed and opens E to 0.61, for an exact error of 2.83. Ours at λ = 10 stops at 0.54, just past E’s wall with zE = 0.09, and its exact error of 2.46 equals that of no repair to within 1%. The inset, on a linear scale, enlarges the three fits next to E’s wall.

The toy layer has three units on a scalar input x, with z1 = x − 1.2, z2 = −0.8x − 0.8 and z3 = 0.6x − 0.12; each unit keeps its colour from Figure 1 (unit 1 purple, unit 2 amber, unit 3 navy). The two monomials tie at x = 1.2, the unit’s wall: to its left the unit outputs 0, to its right it outputs z1. (b) The whole layer. Adding the three outputs is tropical multiplication, ⊙ i(0⊕ zi), and multiplying out gives one line ∑ i∈J zi for each of the 8 subsets J of units (Eq. (5)). The thick envelope is their maximum, which is the layer’s summed output. papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning with a per-unit projector, fitting continual and online learning.
papers.title: A Tropical Geometry View of Forgetting: A Per-Unit Projector for Knowledge-Preserving Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: A gate-aware, per-unit projector uses ReLU activation structure to preserve prior knowledge during replay-free fine-tuning more efficiently than shared-subspace projectors.

papers.abstract: High-resolution vision backbones have long been forced to trade away local token density to afford larger receptive fields. Hierarchical Swin transformers impose this compromise because standard windowed attention materializes an $M^2\times M^2$ score matrix per window, incurring $O(M^4)$ memory as windows or token grids grow. Furthermore, Swin adds a learned relative-position bias elementwise to attention scores, requiring full materialization of the score matrix and its gradient. This keeps Swin and SwinV2 trapped in a small-window($M=8,16$), coarse-token regime with patch size $4\times4$ ($p=4$), limiting performance for fine-grained tasks. We introduce FLASHSWIN, which replaces standard windowed attention with a FlashAttention implementation that computes exact softmax attention without materializing the score matrix, reducing per-window memory from $O(M^4)$ to $O(M^2)$. This enables higher token density and larger receptive fields without inflating memory overhead. Training memory is flat across window sizes: at a $32\times32$ window, FLASHSWIN-T requires only $12.4$\,GB, unchanged from $8\times8$, compared to $70/90$\,GB for SwinV2/V1-T. However, applying FlashAttention directly to Swin creates a trade-off: bypassing the score matrix precludes Swin's additive relative-position bias, forfeiting spatial information in exchange for memory efficiency. FLASHSWIN restores position information as window-local learnable 2D RoPE, making large windows and dense token grids both affordable and accurate. At matched scale, FLASHSWIN-T outperforms Swin variants. With dense tokens and wide windows ($p=2,M=32$), the same Tiny model reaches $84.1\%$ ImageNet-1K, $44.1$ COCO box AP, and $47.28$ ADE20K mIoU---gains of $+1.3$, $+5.1$, and $+1.82$ over SwinV2-T at $M=16$, respectively. At fixed $M=32$, halving the patch size yields roughly $3\times$ larger gains in boundary quality than in mIoU.
authors: Tushar Kataria, Gerald Sabin, Ponnuswamy Sadayappan, Shireen Y. Elhabian
bullets: Standard Swin attention requires O(M⁴) memory per window, limiting receptive fields and token density.
FLASHSWIN computes exact attention without materializing the score matrix, reducing window memory to O(M²).
Window-local learnable 2D RoPE restores positional information lost when removing relative-position bias.
With p=2 and M=32, FLASHSWIN-T achieves 84.1% ImageNet-1K accuracy, 44.1 COCO box AP, and 47.28 ADE20K mIoU.
At M=32, denser tokens improve boundary quality substantially more than overall mIoU.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Token density, architecture, and memory scaling comparison between Swin and FLASHSWIN. (A) An overlapping stem (P = 2) creates dense token grids that preserve spatial boundaries better than standard coarse patches (P = 4). (B) FLASHSWIN replaces Swin’s materialized score matrix and additive relative bias (O(M4) memory) with Window-Local 2D RoPE and a fused FlashAttention [13] kernel. (C) Peak training memory vs. window size M on an H200 GPU (256 × 256 resolution, batch size 128). FLASHSWIN maintains a flat memory footprint as M increases, whereas Swin-V1/V2 grow rapidly and run out of memory at dense settings.

FlashBias-T fuses the kernel but keeps an additive bias as a learned rank-16 factorization: it ties FLASHSWIN on ImageNet (82.65 vs 82.94) yet loses 3.3 box AP, performing at Swin-T’s M=8 level despite M=32.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.
authors: Yanqiao Chen, Yuhan Rui, Dongsheng Hou, Zijie Nie, Yutong Wan, Qi Hao
bullets: Problem: Fixed left-to-right factorization may over-rely on a single chronological prefix during VLA training.
Method: Causally anchored permutation (CAP) samples reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix and trains one policy on subset-conditioned predictions from each expert action chunk.
Contribution: Conditional-set augmentation generates multiple prediction objectives from each demonstration without requiring additional data.
Results: CAP consistently outperforms standard left-to-right training on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation.
Scope: The regularization recipe is also extended to diffusion action generators; a likelihood-agreement diagnostic supports its intended effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: PERMVLA architecture. A pretrained VLM with a Perceiver-style resampler produces context tokens that condition a two-stream action decoder; the sampled reveal order enters only through the attention masks during training, while deployment always executes a chronological action prefix.

Figure 1: Overview of PERMVLA. Autoregressive VLA training conventionally factorizes each expert action chunk in chronological order, so every action slot is always predicted from the same teacher-forced prefix. PERMVLA treats this reveal order as a training-only degree of freedom: the same physical actions are supervised under multiple valid conditioning subsets, while the expert target, action identities, and chronological autoregressive deployment remain unchanged.

Figure 4: Loss construction in PERMVLA. Standard LTR training follows one physical-time factorization and sums teacher-forced per-slot likelihoods against the expert chunk. CAP samples factorization orders over the same physical action variables, illustrated here with K = 1; each order defines revealed subsets and a corresponding likelihood. Their Monte Carlo average is a training-only regularizer of the shared policy. The drawn losses are unnormalized within-chunk sums; Equations 3– 4 define the normalized objectives. Action indices denote fixed physical slots in both panels, and deployment retains deterministic physical-time LTR control.

Figure 5: Illustration of CAP’s theoretical interpretation. In the upper path, a reveal order z defines a normalized joint density qzθ(A | C); substituting this density into the mixed CAP risk Rmix (Equation 16) and minimizing it preserves the expert population target. In the lower path, a demonstrated action chunk creates a family of conditional prediction problems; these problems jointly constrain a finite-capacity model, so features that remain predictive across conditional sets receive repeated support, thereby forming CAP’s regularization mechanism.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is typically framed as acquiring new knowledge without catastrophically forgetting previous tasks. However, a flexible continual learner should also be able to reuse and recombine previously acquired knowledge to rapidly solve novel task compositions. We introduce Gated Target Propagation (GaTaP), a continual learning algorithm in which task-specific gating variables---learned through a closed-form inner loop update---selectively suppress or enhance network modules. Network parameters are learned in a slower timescale outer loop, using the same local difference target propagation error signal as is used for adapting gating variables. We provide tractable experiments on class-incremental learning scenarios for both multilayer perceptron and convolutional network architectures. We show strong performance retention on previously learned tasks, as well as compositional generalization to unseen tasks, achieved through few-shot gain adaptation at inference. We analyze learned gating patterns and find that related tasks exhibit similar gating patterns, suggesting that inferred gates capture meaningful, reusable task structure. Overall, GaTaP provides a powerful framework for jointly ameliorating catastrophic forgetting and enabling few-shot compositional generalization in neural network models.
authors: Abdel Mfougouon Njupoun, Colin Bredenberg, Blake Aaron Richards, Guillaume Lajoie
bullets: Targets continual learners that must both retain prior tasks and recombine learned knowledge for novel compositions.
Learns task-specific gating variables with a closed-form inner-loop update to suppress or enhance network modules.
Updates network parameters in a slower outer loop using local difference target propagation signals.
Experiments cover class-incremental multilayer perceptron and convolutional network settings.
Reports strong retention, compositional generalization via few-shot gain adaptation, and similar gates for related tasks.

papers.abstract: Inference systems determine how fast and how cheaply language models can be served, so making them faster has direct practical value. However, prior work focuses mostly on optimizing certain parts such as kernels or memory within the large system. In this work, we take a holistic approach and apply agentic self-evolution to optimize the whole system end-to-end. Our SEIS (Self-Evolving Inference Systems) autonomously optimizes the entire mini-sglang engine without human intervention through iterative sessions with inherited experiences and code changes. Serving Qwen3-0.6B on H100, the resulting engine reaches 3.27X the throughput of the original mini-sglang implementation and beats SOTA engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang in the single-request workload. The correctness of the optimized inference engine by SEIS is tested in terms of numerical difference and downstream accuracy on math and long-context retrieval tasks. The code and session histories show that the speedup comes from redesigning the whole engine and that building on earlier sessions beats independent attempts. These results suggest that agentic self-evolution can optimize a complex system end-to-end. The evaluation also has to evolve with the engine, and letting agents evolve it is a natural next step.
authors: Zhen Xu, Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Tahseen Rabbani, Ce Zhang
bullets: Targets holistic end-to-end inference-system optimization rather than isolated kernels or memory components.
Iteratively evolves a mini-sglang engine through autonomous sessions that inherit prior experiences and code changes.
On H100 serving Qwen3-0.6B, the optimized engine achieves 3.27× the throughput of the original mini-sglang implementation.
Outperforms vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang in the evaluated single-request workload.
Correctness is assessed through numerical differences and downstream math and long-context retrieval accuracy; evaluation co-evolution remains an open direction.

papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods reuse past experience to improve sample efficiency. However, historical data are typically regarded as off-policy samples for the current policy-improvement update. This work introduces Regularized Dual Averaging Actor Critic (RDA2C), which assigns a distinct role to replay. In regularized dual averaging, the subsequent policy is determined by accumulated policy-improvement feedback, so historical advantage estimates contribute directly to the actor objective rather than solely to the most recent update. RDA2C stores state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, fits a dual score model $Z_\theta$ to the aggregated dataset, and derives the current policy from the accumulated score model using the entropy mirror map. In this way, replay defines an empirical dual objective from which the policy is computed. To analyze RDA2C, we establish a finite-time value-gap decomposition, separating the regularized dual-averaging term from errors due to stale-replay supervised fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay coverage, and stating the assumptions under which each error is bounded. RDA2C accepts advantage labels from any critic. With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on six of eight MuJoCo tasks and eight of twelve Atari games. RDA2C also outperforms AAPDA, the closest dual-averaging baseline, on six of eight MuJoCo tasks. With twin-$Q$ labels, RDA2C matches SAC at matched batch size and update frequency.
authors: Nianli Peng, Geoffrey J. Gordon, Kiant\'e Brantley
bullets: Reframes replay: historical advantage estimates directly shape future policy updates rather than serving only as off-policy samples.
Fits a dual score model to replayed state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, then derives the policy through an entropy mirror map.
Provides a finite-time value-gap decomposition covering stale-replay fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay-coverage errors.
With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on 6/8 MuJoCo and 8/12 Atari tasks, and outperforms AAPDA on 6/8 MuJoCo tasks.
With twin-Q labels, RDA2C matches SAC under matched batch size and update frequency.

papers.title: Policy as Data: Replay-Based Policy Dual Averaging via Advantage Regression

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces core-attention computation, but its indexers still incur repeated selection work and per-layer key-cache storage. Reusing selected indices across layers reduces this overhead but constrains multiple layers to the same token set. We introduce LatentIndex, which extends the latent-sharing principle of Multi-head Latent Attention across indexer layers. Each layer group constructs a shared latent cache from its first layer's hidden states, while layer-specific scoring enables independent token selection. Absorbing key decoders into queries enables direct scoring of the shared cache without reconstructing historical per-layer keys. We develop training-free calibration and investigate a training-aware instantiation of this principle. To balance quality and computation, a hierarchical selection (HS) variant lets followers independently refine a shared candidate set proposed by the anchor. With four-layer sharing, LatentIndex reduces logical indexer-cache storage by 61.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2. Across DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, training-free LatentIndex improves head-wise attention-mass recall over IndexCache by up to 3.28 percentage points while maintaining RULER and LongBench performance close to native DSA. HS further achieves 2.30-2.72 times decode indexer speedups over DSA across 8K-128K contexts, retaining most of LatentIndex's recall. LatentIndex offers a new perspective on cross-layer indexing: sharing continuous representations rather than discrete selections enables efficient reuse while preserving layer-specific token selection.
authors: Zhaohui Wang, Zhixin Pan, Fanxu Meng, Muhan Zhang
bullets: Addresses repeated index-selection computation and per-layer key-cache storage in sparse attention.
Shares a latent cache within layer groups, uses layer-specific scoring, and directly scores shared caches via absorbed key decoders.
Provides training-free calibration and a training-aware variant; hierarchical selection lets follower layers refine shared candidate sets.
With four-layer sharing, reduces logical indexer-cache storage by 61.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2.
Improves attention-mass recall by up to 3.28 percentage points over IndexCache and delivers 2.30–2.72× decode indexer speedups across 8K–128K contexts while largely preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) has consistently played a vital role in advancing science by providing tools to solve fundamental problems encountered in scientific and engineering applications. Over the decades, it has continually evolved to meet the demands driven by successive waves of scientific discovery. For instance, during the 1950s and 1960s, substantial efforts were devoted to developing methods for solving eigenvalue problems that emerged from the rapidly growing field of aerodynamics. This led to the discovery of the LR and QR algorithms. Later the attention turned to the solution of sparse linear systems that were common in applications like computational aerodynamics. Today we are experiencing yet another wave of major scientific advancement and NLA is once more at the heart of its development. This Machine Learning (ML) wave is proving to be utterly disruptive in science and engineering. Many tools in ML particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) are grounded in matrix and tensor methods. As we are approaching Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), it is clear that matrix methods will be called to play an even more significant role. For the numerical linear practitioner the speed of the current change makes it particularly challenging to adapt. This is a survey article that centers on machine learning techniques, with a particular focus on large language models. It has two main objectives. The first is to clarify the core concepts behind Large Language Models in a manner accessible to specialists in numerical methods. The second is to examine the key Numerical Linear Algebra concepts employed by LLM techniques, while also highlighting several significant recent contributions of NLA to the field.
authors: Abdelkader Baggag, Yousef Saad
bullets: Motivates NLA’s renewed importance during the current machine-learning-driven wave of scientific advancement.
Introduces core LLM concepts for readers specializing in numerical methods.
Examines matrix and tensor methods central to LLM techniques.
Highlights significant recent contributions from NLA to machine learning.
Provides context for the growing role of matrix methods as research approaches AGI.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Major milestones in the evolution of artificial intelligence. The timeline highlights selected developments that shaped the field, from early perceptrons and expert systems to deep neural networks, Transformers, and the current era of large language models and generative AI. It is intended as a schematic historical overview rather than an exhaustive chronology.

Figure 5: Components of artificial intelligence: the big picture. The schematic situates large language models within the broader AI landscape and highlights the interplay among core ingredients such as data, optimization, numerical linear algebra, hardware, and software frameworks. Its purpose is to emphasize that modern AI systems emerge from the interaction of several mathematical, algorithmic, and computational components rather than from a single isolated idea.

Figure 2: Growth of parameter sizes in large language models. The plot shows the rapid increase in parameter counts across representative models over time, from early Transformer-era systems to recent frontier models. The horizontal reference lines and the indicated “data wall” emphasize that simple parameter scaling cannot continue indefinitely and may eventually be constrained by data availability and practical training considerations.

Figure 4: Main ingredients of the recent AI wave. The schematic emphasizes the interaction among three mutually reinforcing factors: improved hardware, the availability of large amounts of data, and advances in methods and algorithms. Together, these ingredients explain much of the rapid progress of modern deep learning and large language models.

Figure 3: Order-of-magnitude argument for recent AI progress, adapted from [13]. The figure illustrates the claim that advances in effective compute, algorithmic efficiency, and related “unhobbling” factors may combine multiplicatively, leading to rapid capability gains over relatively short time scales. It is included as a schematic argument about scaling trends, not as a precise predictive model.

Figure 20: Decoder-only Transformer architecture. Repeated masked self-attention and feedforward updates act along a shared residual stream, producing contextual representations used for autoregressive prediction.

Figure 16: Schematic pipeline of a decoder-only large language model. Tokens are mapped to embeddings with positional structure, propagated through repeated Transformer blocks, and finally projected to logits for next-token prediction.

Figure 19: Encoder-decoder Transformer architecture. The encoder computes source-side contextual representations, while the decoder combines masked self-attention and encoder-decoder attention to generate target-side outputs.

Figure 6: A simple multilayer perceptron with three hidden layers. The input vector x is propagated through successive affine transformations and nonlinear activation functions to produce the final output ϕ(x). The figure is intended to illustrate the layered composition that underlies feed-forward neural networks and serves here mainly to establish notation.

Figure 26: Empirical power-law scaling in large language models. Test loss decreases L(N, D) predictably as model size N , dataset size D, and compute budget C increase, following approximate power-law relationships. The schematic summarizes the scaling-law perspective that performance improves smoothly with scale, with diminishing returns captured by the exponents in L(N, D) defined in (3.16.1)

Figure 17: Sinusoidal positional encoding coordinates across dimensions. Each subplot shows the two coordinates P (i, 2j) = sin ( i/100002j/dmodel ) and P (i, 2j + 1) = cos ( i/100002j/dmodel ) as functions of token position i for a representative pair of dimensions. Low-index dimensions vary rapidly with position, while higher-index dimensions vary more slowly, so the encoding provides a multiscale representation of sequence order.

Figure 30: Gradient descent versus natural gradient descent on a two-dimensional Gaussian model with direction-dependent geometry. The left panel shows the decay of the objective L(w) over the iterations, while the right panel displays the corresponding trajectories on the loss surface. Standard gradient descent is slowed by the distorted geometry of the parametrization, whereas natural gradient descent accounts for this geometry through the Fisher metric and converges much more rapidly. Standard (Cauchy) steepest descent is shown by blue plus markers, while natural gradient descent is shown by red circles.

Figure 23: Training and inference in a decoder-only Transformer. During training, the model processes an entire token sequence in parallel and adjusts its weights so that the output probabilities match the target next tokens at all positions. During inference, by contrast, generation is autoregressive: the predicted next token is fed back as input, and the process is repeated sequentially.

Figure 27: Teacher–student knowledge distillation. A pretrained teacher model produces logits and softened output probabilities for the training data, and a smaller student model is trained to match these outputs while also fitting the original targets. The distillation loss transfers information from the teacher’s predictive distribution to the student, allowing the student to imitate the teacher’s behavior with a more compact model.

Figure 18: Pre-LayerNorm Transformer block at layer ℓ. The block applies layer normalization before the attention and MLP sublayers, and writes both outputs additively into the same residual stream. This makes the block an identity-plus-correction map composed of token mixing through attention and channel mixing through the MLP.

Figure 25: Pre-LN Transformer layer as residual-stream accumulation. The input residual stream xℓ−1 is updated by adding the attention-block contribution aℓ and the MLP-block contribution mℓ, giving xℓ = xℓ−1 + aℓ + mℓ. Across layers, the residual stream can be expanded as xℓ = x0 +∑ℓ i=1 ai +∑ℓ i=1 mi, showing how attention and MLP updates accumulate additively through the network.

Figure 12: Recovering an underlying function from noisy data. The figure illustrates the basic problem used to motivate attention: given a cloud of noisy training points (xi, yi), estimate the value of an unknown function at a new query point. In the numerical-analysis viewpoint this suggests interpolation or least-squares approximation, whereas in the machine-learning viewpoint it motivates weighted averaging based on relevance, i.e., attention.

Figure 14: Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression on periodic data. The figure compares an attentionbased kernel-regression estimate with a classical low-degree approximation for an oscillatory target function. In this setting, the similarity-based weighted average captures the periodic behavior more accurately than a simple cubic approximation, illustrating how attention can recover useful structure directly from data when the functional form is not known in advance.

Figure 24: Concentration of pairwise angles in high dimension. The figure shows the distribution of angles between 10,000 random vectors in a 12,288-dimensional embedding space. The sharp concentration around 90◦, together with the narrow 88◦–92◦ band, illustrates the near-orthogonality phenomenon that characterizes random directions in high-dimensional spaces.

Figure 28: Forward step in LoRa. A frozen pretrained weight matrix W0 is augmented by a trainable low-rank update AB, where A ∈ Rd×r, B ∈ Rr×dv , and r ≪ min(d, dv). Instead of updating the full weight matrix, LoRa keeps W0 fixed and learns only the small-rank factors A, and B, thereby reducing the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original forward structure.

Figure 13: Illustration of Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression. Given a query point q, the prediction is formed as a weighted average of the observed values vi, with weights that depend on the similarity between q and the keys ki. This provides a useful bridge to attention, where output representations are likewise obtained by similarity-based weighted averaging.
Figure 29: Illustration of linearized attention. If the softmax is temporarily omitted, the attention map takes the form A (lin)

Figure 7: A simple multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers. The figure illustrates the layer structure used in the classification example and, together with Table 1, helps explain the dimensions of the weight matrices and the total number of trainable parameters.

Figure 8: A simple computational graph for composite-function evaluation. The leaf nodes x, y, and z are primary variables; the intermediate nodes a(x, y, z), b(x, y, z) and c(x, y, z) are derived quantities; and the root node is the target function. The figure illustrates how forward evaluation computes intermediate quantities first, while reverse-mode differentiation (back-propagation) propagates derivatives backward from f to the leaves via the chain rule.

Figure 21: Post-LayerNorm and Pre-LayerNorm Transformer blocks. In the Post-LayerNorm form, normalization is applied after each residual addition, whereas in the Pre-LayerNorm form, it is applied before each sublayer. The comparison highlights that Pre-LayerNorm preserves an exact identity path along the residual stream, which is one reason it is favored in modern LLMs.

Figure 10: A local computational-graph view of one neural-network layer. The figure shows how the pre-activation sℓ = W T ℓ zℓ−1 + bℓ is formed from the previous-layer representation zℓ−1, the weight matrix Wℓ, and the bias bℓ and is then mapped by the activation function σ to produce zℓ. It illustrates how each layer of a neural network can be interpreted as a small computational subgraph whose variables participate in forward evaluation and back-propagation. The circled nodes represent input or parameter variables, whereas the rectangular nodes represent computational operations or derived quantities.

Figure 11: Backward propagation in a multilayer perceptron. The figure schematically illustrates the reverse flow of derivatives through the layered computational graph associated with equations (2.6.9)– (2.6.12). Starting from the loss η, sensitivities are propagated backward through the intermediate states s3, s2, s1 in order to compute gradients with respect to the parameters (W3, b3), (W2, b2), and (W1, b1).

Figure 15: High-level view of autoregressive language modeling. Given a context u < t = (u1, . . . , ut−1), the model assigns a probability distribution to the next token ut, and text generation proceeds by repeating this prediction step sequentially.

Figure 9: Local back-propagation step at an intermediate node in a computational graph. Assuming the partial derivatives of the objective f with respect to the downstream nodes aj, aℓ, and am are already known, the derivative with respect to the current node ak is obtained by applying the chain rule and summing the contributions along all outgoing paths. The figure illustrates the recursive local structure that underlies reverse-mode automatic differentiation.

Figure 22: Generic residual unit in Post-LayerNorm and Pre-LayerNorm form. In both cases the sublayer contributes a learned correction F to the incoming state, but the location of normalization differs: Post-LayerNorm applies normalization after the residual sum, whereas Pre-LayerNorm applies it before the sublayer.

Table 6: Illustrative low-rank concentration of gradient energy. The table shows a normalized singular-value distribution ∑i σi = 1, for which the cumulative energy exceeds 90% within roughly 10 components. Despite the ambient parameter dimension D = 110× 106, most of the gradient energy is concentrated in a very low-dimensional subspace, illustrating the motivation behind low-rank gradient methods.

Table 4: Parameter breakdown of Llama-3 405B by major architectural component. The table decomposes the total parameter count into attention, MLP, embedding/unembedding, and normalization contributions, illustrating that the gated MLP blocks account for the dominant share of parameters in this model.

Table 5: Representative model dimensions illustrating the scale of modern embedding spaces. The table lists the model dimension dmodel for GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, and Llama-3 405B, showing that contemporary large language models operate in ambient spaces of dimension on the order of 104. Such dimensions help explain why many randomly chosen directions are nearly orthogonal, as illustrated in Figure 24.

Table 3: Parameter breakdown of GPT-3 175B by major architectural component. The table decomposes the total parameter count into attention, MLP, embedding/unembedding, and normalization contributions, illustrating that the dense MLP blocks dominate the parameter budget.

papers.abstract: A vision--language--action (VLA) policy can complete complex tasks while ignoring the evidence that should determine its actions. An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target. Language and action show the same pattern: a familiar noun can trigger the operation it was paired with in training even after the verb changes, and a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. We call these dependencies modality shortcuts: regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose Perturbot which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose GroundingFscore, an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while GroundingFscore reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, Perturbot and GroundingFscore provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence.
authors: Mingyu Liu, Chonghao Sima, Tianjian Feng, Hanqing Wang, Cong Chen, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
bullets: VLA policies may succeed by exploiting modality shortcuts instead of evidence needed for the underlying task decision.
PerturbBot uses task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, decision-relevant instruction captions, and relabeled random or failed trajectory segments.
The method changes training while leaving inference unchanged, complementing model scaling by improving the data and signals being scaled.
GroundingFscore provides an offline measure of shortcut reliance alongside task success, helping assess whether scaling is healthy.
The framework aims to preserve responsiveness to task-relevant evidence while disentangling decisions from shortcut priors.

papers.abstract: Soft robots present significant modelling challenges due to their non-linearity, complex dynamics and potentially intricate geometries. These difficulties in accurate system identification and dynamics modelling limit their applications in precise robotics tasks. Prior modelling approaches typically suffer from trade-offs in accuracy, computational efficiency, or speed. The differentiable finite element method (FEM) offers a promising balance between these desiderata for soft robot modelling, and enables the use of gradients for efficient calibration and trajectory optimisation. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end differentiable FEM-based framework designed to streamline modelling and system identification for pneumatic soft robots, enabling the generation of reliable models for downstream tasks. The framework automates the conversion of computer-aided designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes that accurately represent the robot's geometry and actuation mechanism. By integrating easily acquired point cloud data with differentiable FEM, the framework achieves precise identification of material and dynamic actuation parameters using a minimal experimental setup. Additionally, the differentiable nature of the model facilitates trajectory optimisation by leveraging gradients from robot dynamics and contact interactions. We validate the framework by modelling a complex bellow-shaped pneumatic soft robot and demonstrate its efficacy in real-world motion planning tasks. Experimental results indicate high modelling accuracy, with a maximum positional error of less than 3 mm, and successful application in tasks such as path following and grasping.
authors: Shaohong Zhong, Yao Yao, Perla Maiolino, Ingmar Posner
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in modelling nonlinear pneumatic soft robots.
Automatically converts CAD designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes representing geometry and actuation.
Uses differentiable FEM and point-cloud measurements to identify material and dynamic actuation parameters with minimal experiments.
Supports gradient-based trajectory optimisation involving robot dynamics and contact interactions.
Validated on a complex bellow-shaped robot with positional error below 3 mm, achieving path following and grasping.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control architectures are widely used to decompose complex control problems into interacting control levels and are particularly important in robotics, where planning, whole-body motion, and lower-level control must be coordinated across different levels of abstraction and time scales. Their overall closed-loop performance, however, depends strongly on parameters distributed across the hierarchy, such that tuning controllers on different levels independently may neglect relevant cross-layer interactions. We propose a contextual Bayesian optimization framework for joint parameter learning in hierarchical control systems. Rather than modeling closed-loop performance only as a scalar black-box function, we retain separate observations of task performance, realization quality, and control effort. A correlated multi-output Gaussian process models these performance components, while their known aggregation into the overall closed-loop objective is evaluated analytically. The formulation exploits three complementary consequences of hierarchical control: informative performance quantities exposed by the hierarchy, coupling between parameters of different controller levels, and variations of these relations with operating conditions. We evaluate the approach for humanoid loco-manipulation, jointly tuning a centroidal predictive controller and a whole-body controller for physical box pushing under varying box mass. The proposed method achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during both training and adaptation among the considered baselines.
authors: Sebastian Hirt, Lukas Theiner, Jan Peters, Rolf Findeisen
bullets: Independent tuning can miss interactions between parameters at different control levels in hierarchical robotics systems.
The method uses a correlated multi-output Gaussian process and analytically combines predicted performance components into the overall objective.
It exploits hierarchy-exposed metrics, cross-level parameter coupling, and operating-condition-dependent relationships.
Evaluated on humanoid box pushing, it jointly tunes centroidal predictive and whole-body controllers under varying box mass.
It achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during training and adaptation among the evaluated baselines.
