papers.abstract: LLM agents for clinical text-to-SQL applications reason autonomously over multiple steps but cannot assess whether their own reasoning or outputs can be trusted. In high leverage applications such as healthcare, this presents a critical risk where system mistakes can be costly. These reliability failures are also resource failures: an incorrect reasoning trajectory spends computation budget on outputs that must be discarded. We introduce Sentinel, a trajectory-derived, classifier-based confidence layer that analyzes an agent's reasoning, code and database outputs to decide at three points whether to stop: refusing unanswerable questions before the agent runs, halting doomed trajectories mid-run, and withholding untrustworthy answers at delivery. Here, utilizing Chow's rule, we optimize decisions under the EHRSQL shared task's Reliability Score, which penalizes incorrect answers given a utility weighting, and find on the benchmark EHRSQL that Sentinel raises this score from +0.08 to +0.24 when mistakes have a low utility weighting, well above the +0.03 earned by refusing every question, with delivered-answer accuracy rising from 54% to 69% as coverage falls from 84% to 55%. At higher stakes the agents we test rarely answer reliably enough to deliver, and Sentinel detects this on its own, abstaining to that same +0.03 where the unmonitored agent scores -3.02. The same stopping decisions cut computation: at low stakes, where the system still answers, Sentinel eliminates 13-28% of agent steps at little or no reliability cost.
authors: Mincheol Daniel Song, Joshua Ward, Jake Jung, Guang Cheng
bullets: Targets costly, untrustworthy reasoning and outputs in high-stakes clinical text-to-SQL applications.
Uses a classifier-based confidence layer over reasoning traces, code, and database outputs.
Applies Chow’s rule to make stopping decisions before execution, mid-trajectory, and at answer delivery.
On EHRSQL, reliability rose from +0.08 to +0.24 at low utility weighting, while accuracy increased from 54% to 69% as coverage declined from 84% to 55%.
At low stakes, it eliminated 13–28% of agent steps; at higher stakes, it abstained when reliable answers were rarely available.

papers.abstract: Video world models aim to preserve scene structure and predict how dynamic objects evolve beyond visual observations. We present Kepler4D, a framework for future video generation through explicit 4D scene state evolution. Given a monocular video, Kepler4D constructs a shared 3D representation of background geometry, object motion histories, coarse spatial supports, and semantic context. Chain-of-Motion summarizes observed motion and uses a vision-language model to select structured speed and heading decisions and decide whether to bound object-center height from below. A deterministic rollout converts these decisions into future object trajectories for inspection and editing before synthesis. We render the evolving proxies into geometric controls for a pretrained video generator, separating coarse object motion from the synthesis of appearance and articulation. Experiments on real-world videos demonstrate that Kepler4D enables controllable object motion and plausible future rollout while preserving scene consistency.
authors: Feiran Wang, Bin Duan, Junyi Wu, Gaowen Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Builds a shared 3D representation from monocular video, including background geometry, object motion histories, spatial supports, and semantics.
Uses Chain-of-Motion and a vision-language model to select structured speed, heading, and height-bound decisions.
Deterministically rolls out editable future object trajectories before video synthesis.
Renders evolving scene proxies as geometric controls for a pretrained video generator, separating motion from appearance and articulation.
Experiments on real-world videos show controllable object motion, plausible future rollouts, and preserved scene consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Kepler4D. Given an observed video, Kepler4D constructs a structured 4D scene state comprising static scene geometry, foreground motion histories, and semantic context. Chain-of-Motion reasons over the observed motion and scene context to infer structured motion decisions, which a deterministic 3D rollout expands into future object trajectories. These trajectories are rendered with static geometry into depth maps, object control signals, and masks to guide a pretrained video generator. This design separates explicit object motion prediction from video synthesis, enabling controllable generation of future videos while preserving the scene structure.

Figure 4: Automatic future evolution. All methods use the input video without externally supplied object trajectories or motion commands. Methods with camera control are given the same target camera path. Kepler4D depicts the runner moving forward and vaulting over the railing, as in the reference. TrajectoryCrafter shows a viewpoint change without a vault. SPMem shows apparent intersections between the runner and railing. VerseCrafter shows a lateral deviation before the vault.

Figure 3: Static novel view synthesis on DL3DV. We compare Kepler4D with GEN3C, TrajectoryCrafter, and SPMem on indoor and outdoor scenes under target camera motion. Each row shows an input view, the target camera path, the held-out reference view, and the generated results. In these examples, Kepler4D preserves the scene layout and appearance details across viewpoint changes.

Figure 5: Language-guided controllable future generation. Given the same input video, the user specifies the intended motion through a high-level language command. Kepler4D infers an object-level trajectory from the command, shown in the second column. Baselines receive the same language command but not the inferred trajectory or control maps. With explicit trajectory control, Kepler4D better realizes the intended object motion while preserving scene layout and consistency.

Figure 6: Schematic illustration of Chain-of-Motion inputs and outputs. papers.selection_reason: Introduces Kepler4D, a framework for future video generation via explicit 4D scene state evolution. This directly addresses the prediction of environment dynamics and future video generation, a core subtopic of video world models.

papers.abstract: Locomotion on granular slopes such as sand dunes remains a fundamental challenge for legged robots due to reduced shear strength and gravity-induced anisotropic yielding of granular media. Using a hexapedal robot on a tiltable granular bed, we systematically measure locomotion speed together with slope-dependent normal and shear granular resistive forces. While normal penetration resistance remains nearly unchanged with inclination, shear resistance decreases substantially as slope angle increases. Guided by these measurements, we develop a simple robot-terrain interaction model that predicts anchoring timing, step length, and resulting robot speed, as functions of terrain strength and slope angle. The model reveals that slope-induced performance loss is primarily governed by delayed anchoring and increased backward slip rather than excessive sinkage. By extending the model to generalized terrain conditions, we construct failure phase diagrams that identify sinkage- and slippage-induced failure regimes, enabling quantitative risk estimation for locomotion on granular slopes. This physics-informed framework provides predictive insight into terrain-dependent failure mechanisms and offers guidance for safer and more robust robot operation on deformable inclines.
authors: Long Zhao, Xingjue Liao, Feifei Qian
bullets: Measures slope-dependent granular normal and shear resistive forces using a hexapedal robot on a tiltable granular bed.
Finds that normal penetration resistance changes little with slope, while shear resistance decreases substantially.
Develops a robot–terrain interaction model predicting anchoring timing, step length, and locomotion speed from terrain strength and slope angle.
Constructs failure phase diagrams distinguishing sinkage- and slippage-induced failure regimes for quantitative risk estimation.
Provides guidance for safer, more robust locomotion on deformable inclines.

papers.selection_reason: Physics-informed model of legged locomotion and failure on granular slopes; relevant to embodied robot locomotion and terrain interaction.
papers.title: Terrain-Dependent Intra-Cycle Leg Timing for Effective Locomotion on Granular Slopes

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models send each token to a few experts, so each expert is trained on a different part of the data, and this part changes during training. With a shared learning rate, Muon applies updates of roughly the same size to expert matrices of the same shape, even when an expert's update is poorly aligned with its current gradient. We here propose ExpertMuon-Compass (Compass), which multiplies the Muon step of each expert by two factors. A family factor compares the cosine between the expert's orthogonalized update and its gradient with the same cosine for the other experts in its layer. A scalar radius aggregates the alignment between corresponding rows of the update and gradient into one step-length multiplier. Compass keeps the update direction and the momentum buffer of Muon. In pretraining on FineWeb-Edu, Compass with Nesterov momentum on all matrices performs as well as or better than Muon, NorMuon, and other optimizers, with weight decay matched to NorMuon in the longer runs. Adding its factors to NorMuon gives the same or a lower loss than NorMuon. Compass is the most effective when the data seen by each expert varies during training, for example, as when the languages of a multilingual corpus arrive in separate blocks. With Compass, the expert load stays balanced, and the router assigns tokens to experts more decisively. We also prove a perturbation bound for the two factors.
authors: Omatharv Bharat Vaidya, Ashwin Vinod, Pedram Akbarian, Aditya Sai Ellendula, Connor T. Jerzak, Nhat Ho
bullets: MoE experts see different and changing data, making a shared step size poorly suited to all experts.
Compass scales each expert’s Muon update with a layer-relative family-alignment factor and a row-wise scalar radius.
It preserves Muon’s update direction and momentum buffer while modifying only step length.
On FineWeb-Edu pretraining, Compass performs as well as or better than Muon, NorMuon, and other compared optimizers; adding Compass factors to NorMuon matches or improves NorMuon.
Compass is particularly effective under changing expert data, while maintaining balanced expert loads and more decisive routing; the paper also proves a perturbation bound.

papers.title: ExpertMuon-Compass: Alignment-Guided Step Sizes for Mixture-of-Experts Training

papers.abstract: Predicting future spatial states supports collision avoidance and timely decision-making in dynamic environments. However, existing vision-language models (VLMs) and benchmarks for spatial reasoning primarily focus on observed scenes, leaving predictive spatial reasoning beyond the observed interval underexplored. To this end, we introduce SpatialMind, a metric-scale VLM for spatial reasoning and future prediction. Its metric depth adapter anchors spatial reasoning to real-world scale, while its progressive state chain establishes current spatial states and observed dynamics as the foundation for future prediction. Given a video prefix, SpatialMind predicts distances, motion directions, and spatial relations in both observed and unseen future frames. For training and evaluation, we build a scalable data engine that grounds entity descriptions in metric geometry to generate question-answer pairs and state supervision. Using this engine, we construct the SpatialMind-30K dataset and the SpatialMind-2K benchmark, both covering driving and everyday egocentric scenes. The benchmark spans eight tasks across three levels: current-state understanding, observed-dynamics understanding, and future prediction. Experiments show that SpatialMind substantially outperforms both general and spatially specialized models on our benchmark while achieving competitive zero-shot performance on VSI-Bench, OSI-Bench, and VLM4D.
authors: Feiran Wang, Xiaoqi Wang, Ziwei Li, Wenbin He, Yan Yan, Liu Ren
bullets: Addresses the limited focus of existing VLMs and benchmarks on observed rather than future spatial reasoning.
Uses a metric depth adapter for real-world scale and a progressive state chain linking current states and observed dynamics to future predictions.
Predicts distances, motion directions, and spatial relations from video prefixes across observed and unseen frames.
Introduces a scalable geometry-grounded data engine, plus the SpatialMind-30K dataset and SpatialMind-2K benchmark covering driving and egocentric scenes.
Substantially outperforms general and spatially specialized models on its benchmark and achieves competitive zero-shot results on three external benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Model Architecture. Given an observed RGB video and a spatial question, SpatialMind refines metric depth with multiview geometry through global and local corrections. We separately encode metric geometry and camera motion, align their features temporally, and integrate them into visual tokens through cross-attention. The VLM then generates a progressive state chain that grounds the target, establishes its current spatial state, and extends to observed dynamics and future prediction according to the question level before producing the final answer.

Figure 2: SpatialMind Data Engine. We assign each target a distinctive natural-language description through a Select–Describe–Verify process, then combine metric geometry, semantic propagation, and temporal alignment to construct spatial metadata, which supports automatic QA generation across three levels and eight spatial reasoning tasks, with the data distribution shown on the right.

papers.title: From Sight to Foresight: Predictive Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate whether geometrically aligned astronomical representations are also scientifically interchangeable. We analyze every layer's representation from 36 pretrained models using cross-matched optical images, infrared images, and spectra. All 139 analyzed model-survey comparisons show significant local-neighborhood alignment somewhere in the network after accounting for the search over depth. However, alignment does not generally increase with network depth and can be stronger for the changes between consecutive computational blocks than for the block outputs themselves. We find that geometry-selected stages under-perform label-selected stages in every image-transfer comparison; moreover, every final HSC-COSMOS-Web model pair is aligned while every redshift transfer has negative R^2. Models can therefore recover a similar cross-survey geometry among astronomical objects without recovering a survey-invariant linear encoding of the physical properties tested here.
authors: Kshitij Duraphe, Aravind Kannappan, Dun Li Chan, Okiki Famutimi, Yaswant Sai Ejjagiri, Michael J. Smith, John F. Wu
bullets: Analyzes layerwise representations from 36 pretrained models across optical, infrared, and spectral data.
All 139 model–survey comparisons show significant local-neighborhood alignment somewhere in the network.
Alignment does not consistently grow with depth and may be stronger between computational blocks than at their outputs.
Stages chosen for geometric alignment underperform label-selected stages in every image-transfer comparison.
Despite alignment among all final HSC-COSMOS-Web model pairs, redshift transfer yields negative R², challenging the idea that shared geometry implies shared physics.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the transferability of geometric representations versus physical properties in pretrained multimodal models, testing the Platonic representation hypothesis.
papers.title: Shared Geometry Is Not Shared Physics: A Layerwise Test of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Astronomy
papers.tldr: Astronomical models can share local representation geometry without sharing a transferable encoding of physical properties.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability usually studies fully trained models, yet the computations that drive a behaviour can change while the model is still learning the task. On the Indirect Object Identification task, a model should continue with the name mentioned once rather than the name mentioned twice. Pythia models pass through an early training window in which they prefer the repeated name, so accuracy in a choice between the two names falls below one half while language-model loss on a fixed text sample keeps decreasing across the same window. The window reflects a temporary imbalance between two computations. We identify one cause of the wrong preference by selecting a set of attention heads that write the repeated name, on prompts separate from those used for causal evaluation, keeping that selection fixed, and then replacing each head's final-token output with its average output on a separate set of non-repeated-name prompts. This improves the correct-minus-repeated logit difference in a separately trained 160M model and in the official 160M, 410M, and 1B models. At 160M, the head that lowers the repeated name in the mature model shows little of its mature behaviour at this point. It directs less than one percent of its attention to the repeated mention, and its output makes almost no direct contribution to lowering that name's logit. Both properties grow over the interval in which behaviour recovers. Across the 160M, 410M, and 1B models, transplanting the corresponding head's mature parameters into the early checkpoint recovers 35 to 68 percent of the total improvement in the correct-minus-repeated logit difference seen by the end of training. Related early-to-late reversals appear at further Pythia scales, in two independently trained GPT-2 models, and in OLMo. A mature circuit can therefore conceal a transient causal configuration that shaped behaviour earlier in training.
authors: Tejas Dahiya, Cole Blondin
bullets: Pythia models show a below-chance preference for the repeated name even as language-model loss continues to improve.
The error reflects an imbalance between two competing computations, including attention heads that write or suppress the repeated name.
Replacing selected heads’ outputs with averages from non-repeated-name prompts improves the correct-minus-repeated logit difference.
Transplanting mature head parameters into early checkpoints recovers 35–68% of the eventual improvement across 160M–1B models.
Similar early-to-late reversals occur across additional Pythia scales, GPT-2 models, and OLMo.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The suppressing head develops during recovery. Panel A shows that at the 160M floor the head places under one percent of its final-token attention on the repeated mention, rising sharply as behaviour recovers. Panel B shows that the head’s direct output projection on the repeated name is close to zero at the floor and becomes strongly negative later. Panel C shows that transplanting the mature head’s parameters into the early checkpoint moves the logit difference a substantial fraction of the way to the mature value at all three sizes. The effect of replacing this head’s output in the mature model is shown in Figure 31.

Figure 16: Selecting and freezing the copying heads. Four prompt resources play four distinct roles: a selection set for the candidate screen, a validation split held out from that screen, a control-mean set used only after freezing to build the replacement vectors, and an evaluation set. Candidate heads are kept when replacing each on its own improves both the three-name margin and the correct-name probability. The survivors are then ranked on a validation split that took no part in that screen, and the resulting set is frozen and never reselected. Table 3 lists the frozen set for every model. Only afterwards is the intervention effect measured, on evaluation prompts whose names and sentence templates never influenced selection.

Figure 1: The below-chance window. Panel A shows forced-choice accuracy at three model sizes falling below the chance level of one half and then recovering. Panel B shows the mean logit difference over the same interval. Panel A counts the fraction of prompts with positive logit difference, whereas Panel B averages its signed magnitude. The full-vocabulary output at the floor is shown in Figure 8.

Figure 13: Input token edit. The second occurrence of the repeated name is replaced in the token sequence itself, and the model then runs normally. Because repetition status and token identity change together, a positive effect is evidence that the model is sensitive to the repeated relation, not an isolation of repetition alone. This is the only manipulation in the paper that alters the evaluated prompt.

Figure 5: The task and the account in one picture. The upper line shows a prompt with the indirect object mentioned once, the subject mentioned twice, and the position where the model must answer. The lower panels summarise what this paper establishes. Early in training the heads that copy the repeated subject are already causally effective while the head that later suppresses it is close to inert, and the model falls below chance. Later the suppressing computation grows and behaviour recovers.

Figure 11: Residual-stream replacement at the second mention, in two variants. Neither edits the evaluated prompt. Only the activation carried at that position is replaced, after each block in an early layer band. Panel A takes the replacement from a matched control prompt that differs only in the name at the second mention, so the inserted state carries another identity. Panel B instead samples a fresh independent direction for every prompt and every layer, scaling each to the norm of the state it replaces, so no name from any prompt enters. Comparing the two separates disruption of the state from content imported with it.

Figure 28: Activation graft and parameter transplant. Both move something from the mature checkpoint into the floor model, but they move different objects. The graft copies the head’s realised output on the evaluated prompt, so the floor model does not recompute it. The transplant copies the head’s query, key, value and output weights together with its head-specific biases, after which the floor model runs normally and the head computes a fresh output from its own upstream representations. The graft asks whether the mature output is sufficient on these prompts; the transplant asks whether what the head has learned is sufficient inside the early network.

Figure 42: Two models trained on ordinary web text. Panel A shows forced-choice accuracy, panel B the logit difference, and panel C the change produced by replacing the residual-stream state at the second occurrence of the repeated name with the corresponding state from a matched control prompt. The evaluated prompt tokens are unchanged. Run A covers 200000 steps and run B covers 105000 steps.

Figure 38: Controlled task injection. Models are trained from scratch on ordinary text into which task-structured sequences are substituted at a controlled rate, and each checkpoint is then evaluated twice: on names never injected during training, and on names drawn from the injection pool. The gap between the two separates a failure to generalise to unseen names from a failure to learn the task at all.

Figure 29: Cumulative reconstruction at 410M. Mature parameters are transplanted into the floor model cumulatively, beginning with the suppressing head alone and then adding the strongest correct-name writers in order. The result covers selected cumulative prefixes rather than every intermediate count: measurements exist at zero, one, two, three, five and eight writers. The suppressing head alone closes 67.9 percent of the floor-to-mature gap and all eight writers together reach 88.1 percent, at forced-choice accuracy 0.933. The experiment is available at this size only.

Figure 22: The selected head set against two hundred feature-matched control sets, at the official 160M floor in the upper row and the retrained 160M floor in the lower row. The shaded band spans the full range of the two hundred control-set effects and the solid line marks their mean, with the diamond marking the selected set. The control ranges are −0.023 to +0.056 and −0.023 to +0.054 at the official model, and −0.007 to +0.316 and −0.016 to +0.250 at the retrained model. The separation is wide at the official model and narrow at the retrained model.
Figure 7: Language-model loss on the same fixed text sample for the released Pythia 160M model and the separately trained 160M model. Loss decreases across the evaluated checkpoints in both runs.

Figure 6: Language-model loss and IOI forced-choice accuracy around the 160M floor. Loss decreases from steps 1000 to 5000, while IOI accuracy first falls and then recovers. The dashed line marks chance-level forced-choice accuracy.

Figure 9: Vocabulary rank across training at 160M. Median rank of the repeated and correct names across checkpoints, on a logarithmic scale, with rank 1 the highest-scoring token, so a lower rank indicates greater model preference. The repeated name ranks ahead around the floor and the correct name overtakes it during recovery.

Figure 21: The two computations measured on one scale. Each curve is the change in the three-name margin when the same intervention is applied to one of the two frozen head sets, with shaded 95 percent intervals. The left panel uses the retrained 160M model with dense checkpoints through the transition and the right panel uses the released 160M model over full training. A positive value means replacing that set improved behaviour, so the native set was working against the correct answer. A negative value means replacing it damaged behaviour, so the native set was helping.

Figure 2: Position controls at Pythia 160M. Replacing the residual-stream state at the second subject mention reverses sign between the floor and maturity for both the matched and random replacements. The tested interventions at the first subject mention, indirect object, and structural control position do not reverse sign.

Figure 17: Control-mean replacement of the copying heads. The replacement is one fixed vector per head, obtained by averaging that head’s output at the final token over many non-repeated control prompts spanning several names and both name orders. It is therefore not an activation borrowed from a single donor prompt, and it carries no particular competing name. On a separate evaluation prompt in which a name does repeat, each frozen head’s own output is replaced by its fixed mean while every other head, position and parameter is left alone.

Figure 12: Position controls. The norm-matched random replacement of Figure 11 is applied separately at four sites in the same sentence. Values are the change in logit difference at the 160M floor and at maturity. The structural control is defined positionally, as the token immediately following the first subject mention, so the word marked in this example sentence varies across sentence templates. Replacement at the first mention increases the logit difference at both checkpoints, whereas replacement at the indirect object and at the structural control decreases it at both. Only replacement at the second mention changes sign. This is what makes the second-mention state specific rather than one of several positions carrying a causal effect.

Figure 15: How the prompts are divided. After the head set is frozen, the remaining names and sentence templates are split into a control-mean set of non-repeated prompts, used only to build one fixed mean output per head, and an evaluation set of repeated-name prompts on which the effect is measured. The two share no names and no sentence templates, so the measured effect cannot borrow from the prompts that produced the replacement.

Figure 20: Source-position value replacement. The evaluated prompt and the identity at the second mention remain unchanged. For each frozen head, only the value vector read at the first mention is replaced by the corresponding value from a prompt carrying a different name there. If the heads merely wrote toward whichever name repeats, their downstream contribution would be unaffected; if it instead follows the substituted identity, the heads are carrying the name represented at their source. This distinction is what the term copying head refers to.

Figure 27: Mature-head mean replacement, and how it differs from the control mean of Appendix D. Here the selected head’s activation is replaced by its own mean over the prompts and token positions of each sentencetemplate block being evaluated, so the mean comes from the evaluation data itself. In the copying experiment the mean is instead built from a separate set of non-repeated control prompts. The two operations share a word but not a data source, and they answer different questions. Because this head was also chosen by its replacement effect, the size of that effect is selection-conditioned.

Figure 36: First feed-forward block replacement, also called the layer-0 MLP. The evaluated prompt is not edited. A matched control prompt in which no name repeats is run first, the output of that one module is cached, and the cached activation is inserted at the same site in the target run before the forward pass continues. Because the whole module output is replaced, the experiment does not isolate a duplication-specific feature: it establishes the first feed-forward block as an important early source of repetition-sensitive state rather than as a duplication detector.
Figure 8: Full-vocabulary output at the 160M floor. The repeated name receives about twice the probability of the correct name, while greedy decoding produces neither name on almost all prompts.

Figure 10: Repetition sensitivity across nine PolyPythia 160M runs. It shows change in logit difference at each run’s floor after replacing the second occurrence of the repeated name with a different name. All nine effects are positive. These runs are grouped by whether they vary the random seed, the data order, or the parameter initialisation.
Figure 19: Both measures under both resampling procedures. Item-clustered intervals are narrower because the nested procedure additionally resamples a small number of template groups.

Figure 33: Upstream dependence of the mature suppressing head. Panel A replaces the first feed-forward block’s output with its matched non-repeated counterpart and measures the suppressor’s attention to the second mention, which falls at all three sizes. Panel B isolates only the direct connection between the two, adding the first-block difference to the suppressor’s downstream input while holding every other upstream contribution fixed; that route carries none of the attention dependence and well under a tenth of a percent of the logit dependence. The influence therefore reaches the head through intermediate computation, drawn as an unresolved region because the experiments do not identify which components form the path.

Figure 37: Prompt structures for the subject-verb agreement and factual-recall tasks. The subject-verb agreement prompts place an attractor of the opposite number between the subject and the verb position, with the preposition or relative clause varying across templates. The factual-recall prompts state one fact, interpose a second, and then return to the first subject, so the correct continuation is the object belonging to the repeated subject.

Figure 34: The head identified at maturity, traced backward at all three sizes. The upper row shows attention from the final token to the second subject mention and the lower row shows the effect of its output on the repeated-subject logit.

Figure 23: Passive attention split. The total attention a copying head places on the two subject mentions is preserved and divided equally between them, leaving the value vectors untouched. This is neither an ablation nor a value replacement, since the same mass is present and only its allocation changes. The donor attention row is taken, the mass it places on the two subject positions is divided equally between them, and the modified row is written back; every other entry of that row is the donor’s. All seven point estimates satisfy an absolute difference below 0.02, although some uncertainty intervals extend beyond it, so this is a small-effect comparison rather than a demonstration of equivalence.

Figure 30: Magnitude amplification. The floor head’s own output is multiplied by two, four, eight and sixteen, with no mature parameters introduced. If the floor head were already performing the mature operation only weakly, scaling it should move behaviour toward maturity. Accuracy remains below chance at every multiplier, which is why the transplant result is read as supplying a changed computation rather than additional strength.
Figure 39: Held-out accuracy for the four injection rates. The left panel shows the main run and the right panel two further seeds, with seed 43 solid and seed 44 dashed.

Figure 3: Writing the repeated name is causally harmful at the floor. Replacing each frozen head’s promptspecific output at the final token with its control mean improves the correct minus repeated logit difference at all four evaluated floors. Bars are template-to-item nested intervals. The three-name margin is shown in Figure 18.
Figure 14: Decomposition of the input edit at the 160M floor.

Figure 18: Change in the three-name margin of equation 2 from the control-mean replacement. Filled circles indicate that the template-to-item nested interval lies above zero and open squares that it crosses zero. Under item-clustered resampling all four intervals lie above zero.
Figure 40: Final accuracy on the two evaluations for each injection rate in the main run.

Figure 31: Replacing the suppressing head’s promptspecific output with its mature-head mean, taken over the prompts and token positions of each sentencetemplate block. This is not the control mean of Appendix D. The logit difference falls substantially at all three sizes while forced-choice accuracy remains well above chance, so the head is a substantial contributor to the mature preference rather than solely responsible for it.
Figure 24: Interaction term for the repeated-subject logit at each floor setting. An amplification mechanism predicts a positive value.
Figure 41: Ten runs of the minimal task trained from scratch. All ten show the dip and nine show the sign reversal.
Figure 32: Injecting the mature head’s activations into the floor checkpoint, with an output-norm-matched control head as control.
Figure 35: Parameter transplant of the single suppressing head against a bundle of eight randomly chosen heads. The comparison is asymmetric in the number of heads transplanted.
Figure 25: Removing the linearly decoded duplication direction at the 160M floor degrades accuracy in proportion to the removal strength.

Figure 26: Paired differences between the native-routing effect and the passive-split effect, with the analysis bound shaded. Negative values would indicate native routing is more protective than the mechanical split.

Table 3: Sizes in items and the frozen head sets. An item is a name pair evaluated in both orders. The control-mean half and the evaluation half share no names and no templates. Heads are written as layer and index, and the sets are screened, then ranked on a separate validation split, then frozen before the mean is estimated or the effect is measured.

Table 1: Results for the nine PolyPythia 160M variants. Floor accuracy is below the 50% forced-choice baseline for every run. Native and edited LD are measured before and after removing the repeated relation.
Table 2: Change in logit difference from state replacement at each position, at the 160M floor and mature checkpoints.

Table 4: Effect of the control-mean output replacement, in which each frozen head’s prompt-specific output at the final token is replaced by its average output over non-repeated control prompts, with nested resampling intervals. Positive means the preference for the correct name improved.
Table 7: Both measures under both resampling procedures, as 95 percent intervals from ten thousand draws.

Table 8: Paired difference between the native-routing effect and the passive-split effect on the three-name margin. A negative value means native routing is more protective than the mechanical split, which is the direction an additional learned correction would predict. Six of the seven settings are positive, and all seven are smaller in size than the analysis bound of 0.02.
Table 9: The mature-defined suppressing head traced backward at 160M. It is barely engaged by these diagnostics at the floor; they are descriptive, not causal.

Table 10: Change in the floor logit difference when the first feed-forward block’s output is replaced by its matched non-repeated counterpart. The effect is positive at all five sizes and every interval lies above zero.

Table 5: Component logit changes from replacing only the frozen ensemble’s value vectors at the first subject mention, holding the second mention fixed. All four settings use the same source-position value-replacement protocol. The repeated-name logit falls and the substituted name’s logit rises by a comparable amount at every setting, and the three-name margin improves at every setting. Table 6 gives that change under both uncertainty procedures.

papers.selection_reason: Provides mechanistic interpretability insights into LLM training dynamics, relevant to understanding LLM computation and architecture.
papers.title: Copying Before Suppression: What Drives a Below-Chance Dip During Language Model Training?
papers.tldr: During early training, language models temporarily favor the repeated name in Indirect Object Identification because the mature circuit that suppresses it has not yet formed.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLMs can now ingest entire online discussion threads, but understanding their social discourse requires more than reading a long document: models must track parent-reply relations, turning points, scoped subtrees, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories. To test this structure-aware social reasoning, we introduce LongSocialBench, a benchmark of 1,462 verified human-authored multiple-choice items drawn from 94 complete Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView episodes, with a median length of approximately 73K tokens. Each item pairs a complete serialized discussion and reply structure with a four-option question, requiring models to recover structured social evidence. Released items are verified for answerability, option uniqueness, and evidence grounding. Across 18 models and 29 evaluation settings, current long-context workflows remain far below human performance. The best individual result comes from Claude-Opus-4.7, which reaches 63.0% when prompted to eliminate incorrect options before answering, compared with 72.4% for independent human readers. Averaged across all 18 models, the full-context Baseline scores 43.9%. Supplying the gold evidence scope raises this to 55.0%, showing that substantial errors remain even after the relevant thread region is identified. LongSocialBench shows that the missing capability is not context access or prompting alone, but social understanding over structured reply trees.
authors: Xinyi Liu, Rinat Khaziev, Dilek Hakkani-T\"ur, Tarek F. Abdelzaher
bullets: Introduces 1,462 verified multiple-choice questions from 94 complete Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView discussions, with median length of about 73K tokens.
Tests reasoning over parent-reply relations, turning points, subtrees, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories.
Across 18 models and 29 settings, the best result is 63.0% for Claude-Opus-4.7 with option-elimination prompting, versus 72.4% for human readers.
The full-context baseline averages 43.9%; providing the gold evidence scope improves performance to 55.0%, but leaves substantial errors.
Finds that the central limitation is social understanding over structured reply trees, not merely context access or prompting.

papers.title: LongSocialBench: Do Long-Context LLMs Understand Online Discussion Threads?
papers.tldr: LongSocialBench shows that long-context LLMs still struggle to understand the structured social dynamics of online discussion threads, despite being able to process their full length.

papers.abstract: Real-world time series are frequently driven by exogenous events and structural shifts, rendering conventional forecasting based solely on historical numerical observations insufficient. While language models can retrieve external news, standard retrieval-augmented approaches struggle with high noise, missing signals, and an inability to reason causally about event impacts. We propose SEER (Self-Evolving Event Reasoning and Retrieval), a closed-loop framework that dynamically optimizes event conditioning for time series forecasting. SEER translates prediction errors into two decoupled feedback mechanisms: (i) a reflective retrieval memory that refines subsequent search queries and filters spurious noise, and (ii) a persistent causal knowledge base that distills transferable domain dynamics. SEER enforces strict chronological boundaries across both event retrieval and reflection, preventing look-ahead bias and data leakage. Across six volatile time-series benchmarks, SEER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time series foundation models and language model baselines.
authors: Mingtian Tan, Palash Goyal, Mihir Parmar, Sarkar Snigdha Sarathi Das, Chun-Liang Li, Nanyun Peng, Thomas Hartvigsen, Jinsung Yoon, Tomas Pfister
bullets: Targets forecasting failures caused by exogenous events, structural shifts, noisy retrieval, and missing signals.
Uses a closed-loop process with two feedback paths: reflective memory for better event queries and noise filtering, plus a persistent causal knowledge base.
Maintains strict chronological boundaries during retrieval and reflection to prevent look-ahead bias and data leakage.
Consistently outperforms time-series foundation models and language-model baselines across six volatile benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of the SEER framework. At step 𝑡, an LLM Forecaster ( 𝑓) generates a reasoning process 𝑟𝑡, which contains the prediction ?̂?𝑡, based on historical numerical data 𝑥𝑡 and a dynamic textual context space. This context space supplies the LLM with augmented external events (further retrieved using Mret 𝑡 and filtered via reflective memory Msel 𝑡 ) alongside persistent causal knowledge K𝑡. Upon observing the true outcome 𝑦𝑡, SEER closes the feedback loop by reflecting on the prediction error. The updates are decoupled: Φmem refines the Event-Augmented Memory M𝑡+1, while Φknow extracts transferable domain dynamics from past errors to form K𝑡+1.

Figure 3 | SEER transfers to non-time-series forecasting. papers.abstract: Accelerating the prediction of long-term behavior in chaotic systems is crucial in scientific computing. However, existing methods rely on numerical solvers or autoregressive models that advance one small step at a time, which makes long horizons expensive. We instead view this problem as learning the system's time-invariant evolution operator, which jumps the state across a large time span in a single evaluation. To this end, we derive the consistency equations a time-invariant operator must satisfy, with differential and compositional objectives in physical time. These equations also connect the learned operator to the physics-prescribed instant dynamics, enabling physics embedding in consistency learning. Across five chaotic systems, we find that physics-distilled consistency makes both short-term trajectories and long-term statistics more accurate. The learned operator survives temporal extrapolation and requires one-tenth as many evaluations as autoregressive rollout, offering an efficient route to long-term simulation of chaotic dynamics.
authors: Lufang Chiang, Jiachen Yao, Thomas Y. L. Lin, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Targets the high cost of numerical solvers and autoregressive models that advance chaotic dynamics one small step at a time.
Derives differential and compositional consistency equations for time-invariant evolution operators in physical time.
Embeds instant dynamics prescribed by physics into consistency learning through physics distillation.
Across five chaotic systems, improves short-term trajectories and long-term statistics, with temporal extrapolation capability.
Uses one-tenth as many evaluations as autoregressive rollout, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) Autoregressive models and neural ODEs advance in small steps and need many NFEs. (b) We propose consistency conditions for a time-invariant operator that jumps any ∆t in one step. (c) The model itself or the governing equations supply the velocity in these conditions.

Figure 3: Consistency strength. Validation relative L2 error against the consistency weight, as a fraction of the data-only model’s error, averaged over the five systems. E-phys and L-phys are fed the governing equations; the other three are fed the model’s own velocity.

papers.abstract: Model compression strategies are widely employed to reduce memory footprint and network complexity, particularly for devices with constrained computational, memory, and energy resources. Prior works that rely on simultaneous conversion from floating-point high-precision (FP32) to integer low-precision (INT4) representations and distillation into smaller models suffer from unstable training and drastic degradation of prediction performance. To address these limitations, we propose a unified framework, known as \textbf{P}rogressive \textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}ncestor \textbf{B}it-depth \textbf{D}istillation (PMABD), that progressively compresses the network while transferring knowledge through a growing pool of higher-precision ancestor teachers. PMABD generates a sequence of intermediate teachers that each learn from all higher-precision ancestors and jointly supervise the final target student. This multi-ancestor, multi-stage design stabilizes ultra-low-bit quantization by lowering quantization noise profiles across training and ensuring stable quantization. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-20/32/18, and Tiny-ImageNet with MobileNetV2 show that PMABD outperforms state-of-the-art compression frameworks, results in 1.06$\%$ increase in performance of W2A2 (ResNet-18/CIFAR-100) student model. We show that a saturation-based stopping criterion contributes to improve the performance of our final student.
authors: Adil Mubashir Chaudhry, Osama Ahmad, Zubair Khalid, Murtaza Taj
bullets: Addresses unstable training and severe performance loss from direct FP32-to-INT4 compression and distillation.
Builds intermediate teachers progressively, with each learning from all higher-precision ancestors.
Uses multi-stage, multi-ancestor supervision to reduce quantization noise and stabilize training.
Evaluated on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet across ResNet and MobileNetV2 models.
Reports a 1.06 percentage-point performance increase for a W2A2 ResNet-18 student on CIFAR-100; saturation-based stopping further improves the final student.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: PMABD block diagram illustrating the progressive loop. A shared model pool aggregates logits and feature-map knowledge from multiple ancestor teachers to guide the student model, PMABD loss function LPMABD leads the training phase of the model. Is Training Done? signifies that each model is trained until early stop criteria is achieved. Is Termination condition? provides deployable final model if our desired precision model is acquired and accuracy is saturated between two consecutive models at same precision. Teachers are fake-quantized, so their logits and features are FP32 tensors; aggregation is done in FP32.

Fig. 2: Filter-normalized loss landscape comparison. (a) and (c): Direct W4A4 distillation yields a sharp, irregular, and highly convex minimum. (b) and (d): PMABD W4A4 distillation produces a demonstrably flatter, smoother, and wider basin, explaining its robustness to quantization noise.

papers.abstract: Language models exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet adapting them to structured domains remains challenging and can yield inconsistent outcomes. We identify representation compatibility, the extent to which a model effectively processes a representation for a structured task, as a key factor in adaptation. We study this in chess, which provides a controlled testbed with precise semantics, computable optimal actions, and multiple state representations, including a symbolic encoding (FEN) and a spatial format (ASCII). We find that models often process semantically equivalent inputs substantially differently, affecting both learning and generalization. Building on this observation, we propose representation-aligned auxiliary supervision, which uses environment-derived tasks expressed in compatible representations to improve adaptation to structured domains. Across models and representations, auxiliary supervision consistently improves optimal-move prediction relative to target-only training under identical target data. Tasks that expose environment dynamics provide larger and most consistent gains than surface-level or static supervision, while remaining competitive with substantially increasing the amount of target-task data. Moreover, ASCII-trained models transfer more effectively to FEN than FEN-trained models do to ASCII, even surpassing the FEN target-only baseline on FEN evaluation. The gains also extend beyond optimal-move prediction to open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation. Overall, our results show that auxiliary supervision in model-compatible representations can enable effective adaptation in structured domains.
authors: Kyuyoung Kim, Peiyao Sheng, Ashwin Hebbar, Peiyang Xu, Yunfei Xie, Kevin Wang, Rui Xin, Chen Wei, Zhangyang Wang, Jinwoo Shin, Pramod Viswanath, Sewoong Oh
bullets: Chess provides a controlled testbed with equivalent symbolic (FEN) and spatial (ASCII) representations.
Semantically equivalent representations can produce substantially different learning and generalization behavior.
Environment-dynamics supervision yields larger and more consistent gains than static or surface-level tasks.
Auxiliary supervision improves optimal-move prediction with the same target data and remains competitive with adding much more target data.
Benefits extend to grounded commentary generation, while transfer from ASCII to FEN is stronger than the reverse.

(b) Optimal-move accuracy under matched-data auxiliary supervision conditions. All results use Qwen314B, with models trained and evaluated in either FEN or ASCII.

Figure 2: Representation compatibility in next-state prediction. Across model scales and families, ASCII inputs consistently yield higher board accuracy (left) and format compliance (right) than FEN prior to domain adaptation. The gap narrows with model size but remains substantial.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding models can enhance radiology workflows by linking report findings to image regions. This is particularly valuable for 3D CT, where findings often occupy a tiny fraction of the volume. Training 3D grounding models requires large sets of paired phrases and regions, and building such datasets is expensive, requiring radiologists to annotate images by hand. We posit that this supervision is already created implicitly during routine reporting, as radiologists frequently place 2D annotations (e.g., distance measurement, arrows) on key images to make measurements and to support report interpretation. We introduce an automated pipeline that converts these routine clinical annotations into large-scale phrase-region supervision for 3D visual grounding. The pipeline links each annotation to the corresponding finding in the report through metadata matching, then uses a promptable 3D segmentation model to convert the 2D annotation into a volumetric mask. This produces phrase-mask-volume datasets without requiring additional radiologist annotation. Applied to a single institution's clinical picture archiving and communication system (PACS), our approach generated 105K phrase-mask-volume triplets from 59K abdominal CT exams. We also introduce two abdominal CT grounding benchmarks, LocusBench-Onc and LocusBench-ED, which comprise 240 oncology and 260 emergency-department radiologist-reviewed phrase-mask-volume triplets, respectively, with the latter spanning 13 distinct categories such as appendicitis, hematoma, and hernia. We further introduce LocusCT, a 3D visual grounding model trained on this dataset, which achieves hit rates of 0.725 on LocusBench-Onc and 0.773 on LocusBench-ED, substantially outperforming comparator models. These results show that routine PACS annotations are a scalable, previously unused source of supervision for 3D visual grounding.
authors: Sam Church, Danyal Maqbool, Joshua D. Warner, Andrew Voter, Junjie Hu, Meghan G. Lubner, Tyler J. Bradshaw
bullets: Addresses the cost and scarcity of paired phrase–region annotations for 3D CT grounding.
Links 2D PACS annotations to report findings using metadata, then expands them into 3D masks with a promptable segmentation model.
Generated 105K phrase–mask–volume triplets from 59K abdominal CT exams at one institution.
Introduces radiologist-reviewed LocusBench-Onc and LocusBench-ED benchmarks, plus the LocusCT grounding model.
LocusCT achieved hit rates of 0.725 and 0.773 on the oncology and emergency-department benchmarks, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Our method provides large-scale, report-linked supervision for 3D CT grounding. (a) Composition of the training data for VoxTell and LocusCT. We call a volume report-linked if its segmentation masks are paired with finding phrases from the exam’s own clinical report. Only 5% of VoxTell’s volumes (13% of its CT volumes) are report-linked, whereas all 65K volumes (from 59K exams) in LocusCT’s training set are. (b) Distribution of the 105K findings across the 20 most frequent categories, which together cover 88.1% of all findings.

Figure 4: LocusCT predictions on LocusBench-Onc and LocusBench-ED. Each example shows a clinical finding description alongside a representative CT slice with the model prediction (red), radiologist-annotated ground truth (green), and Dice score.

Figure 2: Automated generation of phrase–mask–volume triplets from routine clinical data. An LLM extracts finding information from free-text reports, which are matched to 2D GSPS annotations using exam metadata. A promptable 3D segmentation model converts the matched 2D annotation into a volumetric mask, yielding grounding supervision without additional radiologist annotation.

Figure 1: Visual grounding of clinical findings in 3D abdominal CT. A radiology report contains multiple findings referring to distinct anatomical regions within the CT volume. Colored phrases in the report correspond to their respective localized regions in the 3D abdominal CT, illustrated by the matching colored boxes and volume crops.

Figure 5: LocusCT predictions on the external Merlin dataset. Report phrases (left) and predicted masks in red (right), across eight ED categories. Merlin has no mask annotations, so these examples are qualitative only.

Figure 8: Per-category Dice scores for LocusCT on LocusBench-ED, sorted by median Dice. Each category contains 20 cases (shown in parentheses). Points are individual cases, boxes span the interquartile range, and black lines mark the median. Many categories are bimodal: most cases are segmented well, but some score near zero, meaning the model failed to localize the target finding at all rather than producing a poor boundary. Performance is strongest for mass, aneurysm, and cyst and weakest for diverticulitis and abscess.

Figure 6: Representative GSPS to 3D segmentation failure modes. Yellow marks show the radiologist’s GSPS annotation, magenta shows the predicted mask, and the matched report sentence (partial) appears below each panel. (a) Shifted, minor error: the mask covers the correct nodule but is offset slightly from the annotation. (b) Shifted, major error: the mask lands on nearby tissue and largely misses the annotated pancreatic mass. (c) Misread arrow: instead of the small lesion at the arrow tip, the mask segments a larger adjacent structure. (d) Off-body: the annotation falls outside the patient, and the mask fragments across background noise.

Figure 9: Reader study of LocusCT grounding on the external Merlin dataset. For each of the 13 LocusBench-ED finding types, six abdominal CT scans from the Merlin dataset were grounded with LocusCT using the corresponding report phrase, and each predicted mask was rated by a boardcertified radiologist on a 5-point scale (1 = Missing/Not near the object of interest; 2= Incorrect, but near the object of interest; 3 = Useful for localization, but not for information extraction; 4 = Useful, only minor edits required for clinical measurements; 5 = Very useful: could be used for clinical measurements). Bars show the distribution of ratings per finding type, sorted by mean rating. Hatched segments mark cases where the model produced no prediction; these are assigned a score of 1 and included in the means. The bottom row pools all 78 cases.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks continue to grow in parameter count, driving up training and inference cost on GPUs. Sparse neural networks and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) promise to reduce these costs, but most implementations rely on binary masks over dense tensors and recover little of the theoretical compute, memory, or energy savings. We propose SNACK, a truly sparse GPU layer that stores and computes only non-zero connections. SNACK exposes a simple PyTorch API for restructuring connections and backpropagating gradients entirely in the sparse paradigm, and ships SNACK-COO, a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel with a batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping tuned for the small-batch, high-sparsity regime typical of large-model training and single-stream inference. At the kernel level, SNACK is up to 7x faster than the masked dense baseline (Dense+Mask) and competitive with cuSPARSE, Sputnik, and FlashSparse at 95% sparsity. At 90% sparsity, a single SNACK layer accelerates training by 8x and 3.7x, and inference by 4x and 2x, over Dense+Mask and fully dense layers, respectively, while using 72% less memory than dense and substantially less energy. End-to-end, SNACK reduces GPT-2 peak training memory by up to 40% and graph-style inference latency by 4.8x over Dense+Mask at 99% sparsity.
authors: Jafar Badour, Maurice van Keulen, Elena Mocanu
bullets: Addresses the limited practical benefits of masked sparse and dynamic sparse training implementations that still use dense tensors.
Provides a PyTorch sparse-training API and SNACK-COO, a custom CUDA SpMM kernel optimized for small batches and high sparsity.
At 95% sparsity, the kernel is up to 7× faster than Dense+Mask and competitive with several sparse baselines.
At 90% sparsity, layers achieve up to 8× faster training and 4× faster inference than Dense+Mask, with 72% lower memory use than dense layers.
End-to-end results include up to 40% lower GPT-2 peak training memory and 4.8× lower graph-inference latency at 99% sparsity.

papers.abstract: Generating a boundary representation (B-rep) conditioned on a single image requires faithful reconstruction of geometry, valid topology, and support for complex shapes. We present UniBRep, a geometry-first framework that adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model to generate a feature mesh as a unified intermediate representation. Its surface provides a geometric scaffold, while spatially aligned learned features encode face-separation cues for topology recovery. Dual decoder branches generate the geometry and face-separation features; a geometry- and feature-guided construction pipeline then fits parametric surfaces, recovers boundary curves and connectivity, and assembles an explicit B-rep using a CAD kernel. Recovering topology from mesh regions avoids predefined architectural face-count limits, allowing face count to scale with shape complexity. On the standard DeepCAD benchmark, UniBRep produces valid B-reps for 80.49\% of inputs and reduces face Chamfer distance from 0.1096 to 0.0345 relative to CADDreamer. In a matched comparison, UniBRep also outperforms the HoLa public demo across all reported metrics. Further evaluations demonstrate scalability to high-complexity shapes beyond the standard 30-face range, generalization to objects outside the CAD training distribution, and qualitative transfer to real photographs.
authors: Haiyang Ying, Allen Tu, Jiaye Wu, Tom Goldstein, Matthias Zwicker
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reconstructing faithful geometry and valid topology from a single image.
Adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model to produce a geometry-first feature mesh with topology-relevant face-separation cues.
Uses dual decoders and a geometry-/feature-guided pipeline to fit parametric surfaces, recover boundaries and connectivity, and assemble explicit B-reps.
On DeepCAD, achieves 80.49% valid B-rep generation and lowers face Chamfer distance from 0.1096 to 0.0345 relative to CADDreamer.
Scales beyond the standard 30-face range and shows generalization beyond CAD training data, including qualitative transfer to real photographs.

papers.abstract: Coding agents operating under ambiguous instructions or user prompts must decide whether to ask clarifying questions or attempt a solution directly. While clarification from the user may improve the correctness of the agent's solution, each back-and-forth interaction incurs user and system costs, forming an explicit accuracy vs. efficiency tradeoff. Existing works study clarification behavior but do not train policies under enforceable clarification budgets; penalty-based approaches typically require separate coefficient tuning swept across all clarification budget levels. We formulate clarification as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and post-train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with PPO-Lagrangian to optimize coding accuracy, subject to an expected question-budget constraint. Evaluated on HumanEvalComm with a GPT-4o-mini oracle simulator, the resulting policies reveal that untuned clarification behavior is Pareto-inefficient: budget-constrained policies can simultaneously achieve higher accuracy and lower clarification rates than the baseline model. Across budget levels, we observe a log-shaped Pareto frontier with diminishing returns to additional clarification. Gains arise not from simply asking more questions overall, but from improved question targeting and better code generation under ambiguity. Without explicit supervision, trained policies learn to allocate clarification budget non-uniformly, asking more frequently on tougher (multi-degradation) tasks. These results suggest that unconstrained interactive LLM systems may systematically use clarification inefficiently.
authors: Abhinav Rajput, Acey Vogelstein
bullets: Frames clarification in coding agents as a constrained Markov Decision Process balancing accuracy against interaction cost.
Post-trains Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with PPO-Lagrangian under an expected question-budget constraint.
On HumanEvalComm with a GPT-4o-mini oracle simulator, constrained policies can outperform the baseline in both accuracy and clarification efficiency.
The accuracy–clarification tradeoff follows a log-shaped Pareto frontier with diminishing returns from additional questions.
Policies learn to target clarification toward harder, multi-degradation tasks rather than asking more uniformly.

papers.abstract: Before autonomous driving systems can be deployed on public roads, it is vital that these systems comply with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms. Although neural networks trained on large amounts of driving data perform well in routine driving tasks, these models often struggle in novel situations that are not well-represented in the data. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines a neural network for intuitive, learning-based planning in routine driving tasks with model predictive control for reasoning-based planning in unfamiliar situations, inspired by Dual Process Theory. A meta-cognitive component is designed to switch between the two, using a knowledge graph to reason about contextual risk based on explicit perceptual information and relevant traffic rules and social norms. Contextual risk is represented through risk fields, guiding both the switching mechanism in the meta-cognitive component and compliance with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms in the reasoning-based planner. The effectiveness of our framework is tested in CARLA for variations of a typical out-of-distribution situations involving (emergency) vehicles running a red light. We show that the novel architecture reduces the number of collisions in the scenarios by 89% and improves compliance with the special right-of-way rules, compared to the NN-only planner.

papers.abstract: Radiance fields, implemented with either implicit (NeRF) or explicit (Gaussian Splatting) representations, are advancing the state of the art in novel view synthesis at a rapid pace. Even though the rendered views they generate are often compelling, they are not free of errors. In this paper, we propose a new approach for pixel-wise uncertainty quantification based on measuring the inconsistencies among renderings by the radiance field model in virtual cameras sampled near the target viewpoint. We named our approach VCURF for Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields. VCURF treats the radiance field model as a black box, only assuming that it is capable of rendering color and depth on demand. This property makes our approach applicable to both NeRF and GS models without any modification. Our experiments on a combination of datasets, radiance field models and baselines demonstrate VCURF's effectiveness in pixel-wise uncertainty estimation. We conclude the paper with findings that question the way view selection is tackled by the majority of the current literature.
authors: Liyan Chen, Nathaniel Burgdorfer, Philippos Mordohai
bullets: Addresses errors and uncertainty in novel views generated by NeRF and Gaussian Splatting models.
Samples virtual cameras around the target viewpoint and compares their rendered outputs.
Treats the radiance field as a black box requiring only on-demand color and depth rendering.
Applies to both implicit and explicit radiance-field representations without model modification.
Experiments across datasets, models, and baselines demonstrate effective pixel-wise uncertainty estimation and raise questions about common view-selection strategies.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have enabled generalist control policies capable of completing a wide range of tasks. However, their performance degrades when deployed in unseen environments, making it critical to detect failures and teach recovery behaviors. Existing runtime monitoring methods often require task- and policy-specific training or hyperparameter tuning, limiting cross-task deployment and introducing additional overhead during iterative policy updates. We present Reward-DAgger, a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to determine when human intervention is needed. Our approach is agnostic to the underlying policy architecture, requires no access to policy internals, and can be applied across tasks without retuning the gating mechanism. Our results show that Reward-DAgger achieves a better failure-detection accuracy-latency tradeoff than existing runtime monitoring baselines. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, Reward-DAgger consistently improves the downstream policy's autonomous success rate throughout interactive learning and achieves strong return on human effort, outperforming the baselines in most settings. Importantly, the same gating configuration is used across tasks without task-specific hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating transfer across tasks, environments, and policy architectures. Code and videos are available at https://liralab.usc.edu/reward-dagger.

papers.abstract: Shape from shading using a single image of a Lam- bertian surface is inherently ambiguous. When the light source direction is known, the surface normal estimation has a cone- ambiguity, which worsens when the source is unknown. Recently, shape from heat conduction has emerged as an approach that leverages heat transport equations to estimate the Shape Lapla- cian operator, an intrinsic measure of shape. However, deriving surface normals from the Laplacian operator encounters a local binary convex/concave ambiguity. Our contribution introduces a novel theory to resolve these local shape ambiguities (excluding a few degeneracies) without relying on priors like smoothness, by combining the cues from shading and heat conduction. Our method ensures the mathematical constraints of both shading and the Laplacian are satisfied simultaneously, even with an unknown light source. We validate our theory through simulations of complex shapes and analyze its performance in the presence of noise, as well as on a noisy single thermal video of real-world objects with complex shapes and material properties, including varying albedo.
authors: Akihiko Oharazawa, Sriram Narayanan, Mani Ramanagopal, Srinivasa G. Narasimhan
bullets: Addresses ambiguities in single-image Lambertian shape-from-shading and heat-conduction reconstruction.

Validated on simulated complex shapes under noise and on a noisy real-world thermal video with varying albedo.
Studies robustness to noise and complex material properties.

papers.abstract: A language model reads long text in one quadratic forward pass, stops at the context window, and loses accuracy with length before reaching it. We ask whether the read can be factorized when deciding over a finite set: which document is relevant, which option is supported, which passage is the evidence. Periscope, a training-free inference method, arranges the $N$ chunks of a text on a $K{\times}K$ grid with $K{=}\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil$ and asks a frozen model the same question about $K$ local spans of consecutive chunks and $K$ strided spans that sample the whole text, reading the log-odds of every answer at one token. Each answer takes its best local and strided score, and scoring every chunk by its two spans gives an evidence map at no further cost, whose peak is the chunk behind the answer. Every probe is about $\sqrt{sc}$ tokens for a text of $s$ tokens and chunk size $c$, so a window of $W$ tokens reaches $W^{2}/c$ tokens at $s^{1.5}$ cost. The map replaces the long read. On LongBench v2, reading only the $K$ chunks the map ranks highest, 9k tokens, matches the same model's best window read across windows from 32k to 1M tokens, and on InfiniteBench, where the median context is 150k tokens, it leads the best window read by 5 points. The same map ranks BRIGHT's long-document corpora with the best NDCG@10 of six methods. Each call caches only one probe, so a 27B model reads 4.5M-token contexts on one 80GB GPU, where a single pass would need 296GB of cache. A long read then needs a GPU that holds the model, not one that holds the text.

papers.abstract: The quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) forces a trade-off between spatial resolution and rollout horizon, particularly for fine-scale PDEs where shocks, reaction fronts, and material interfaces occupy small, evolving regions of the domain. Conventional neural surrogates also lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically. We propose WAMRViT, a ViT that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion, jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings, and regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and lets the model learn across resolution levels. Unlike fixed-budget adaptive-tokenization methods, WAMRViT imposes no predetermined token count and supports fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout. To our knowledge, it is the first machine-learning surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over a finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged full-field and refined-region accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, its end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and approximately token-matched coarser-patch ViTs. On a complex AMR combustion problem whose finest features cannot be represented natively by the evaluated uniform-grid baselines, WAMRViT operates directly on adaptive cells and substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity. authors: Yilin Zhuang, Noah Zambrano, Karthik Duraisamy

Improves refined-region accuracy with fewer tokens, while the multi-scale model achieves the best reported first-step and long-horizon accuracy across the evaluated benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Applications such as engineering design often require us to optimize a black-box function, i.e., a system whose inner processing is not analytically known and whose gradients are not available. Practitioners often have a fixed budget for the number of function evaluations and the performance of an optimization algorithm is measured by its simple regret. In this paper, we study the class of "Optimistic Optimization" algorithms for black-box optimization that use a partitioning scheme for the domain. We develop algorithms that learn a good partitioning scheme and use flexible surrogate models such as neural networks in the optimization procedure. For multi-index functions on an $m$-dimensional subspace within $d$ dimensions, our algorithm attains $\tilde{O}(n^{-\beta / d})$ regret, where $\beta = 1 + \frac{d-m}{2m-1}$, as opposed to $\tilde{O}(n^{-1/d})$ for SequOOL, a state-of-the-art optimistic optimization algorithm. We use our approach to improve the quality of Activation-aware Weight Quantization (AWQ) of the OPT-1.3B model, achieving $\sim10\%$ improvement in performance relative to the best possible unquantized model.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have shown strong performance in volumetric segmentation, but their effectiveness on clinical CT is limited by an isotropic Euclidean lattice assumption. This conflicts with anisotropic CT acquisition, leading to two key issues: (1) a metric mismatch between voxel indices and physical anatomy, and (2) accuracy degradation from isotropic resampling. To address this, we propose MAGEFormer, a geometry-calibrated framework that embeds physical metric constraints directly into representation learning. Our method introduces Metric-Adaptive Spatial Embedding (MASE) to calibrate positional frequencies using voxel spacing, Geometry-Constrained Attention (GCA) to suppress physically implausible feature correlations, and Geometric View Voting (GVV) to reduce discretization bias during inference. We evaluate MAGEFormer on two multi-organ abdominal CT benchmarks, BTCV and FLARE 22, under a unified protocol against strong CNN and Transformer-based baselines. MAGEFormer achieves the strongest boundary accuracy among the compared methods, with 10.58 mm HD95 on BTCV and 3.40 mm HD95 on FLARE 22, and shows consistent gains in Dice under the same protocol. These results show that geometry-aware internal calibration is more effective than relying on conventional isotropic preprocessing alone for anisotropic CT segmentation.
authors: Jiaying Li, Paolo Remagnino
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between isotropic ViT assumptions and anisotropic CT anatomy, avoiding reliance on isotropic resampling alone.
Uses Metric-Adaptive Spatial Embedding, Geometry-Constrained Attention, and Geometric View Voting to calibrate features and reduce discretization bias.
Evaluated on BTCV and FLARE 22 under a unified protocol against CNN and Transformer baselines.
Achieves strongest boundary accuracy among compared methods, with HD95 of 10.58 mm on BTCV and 3.40 mm on FLARE 22, alongside consistent Dice gains.

papers.abstract: Data assimilation combines model forecasts with noisy, incomplete observations to estimate the evolving state of a dynamical system. Existing methods face two compounding challenges: high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics make repeated forward simulation computationally expensive, while sparse observations provide limited direct information about the full state. To address these challenges, we propose the Latent-Dynamics Ensemble Flow Filter (LD-EnFF), a sequential Bayesian filtering framework that performs both forecast propagation and filtering updates in a compact latent space. LD-EnFF combines a latent dynamics surrogate for ensemble propagation with a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based observation model that evaluates a state-dependent observation likelihood in latent space. At each assimilation step, an ensemble filtering update based on flow matching uses the forecast ensemble and this likelihood to generate posterior samples, jointly updating latent states and uncertain parameters. This design avoids repeated full-state simulation during forecasting and full-field reconstruction during likelihood evaluation. LD-EnFF substantially outperforms a broad range of data assimilation algorithms on benchmarks spanning Kolmogorov flow, tsunami propagation, and atmospheric modeling, all featuring complex dynamics and sparse, noisy observations.
authors: Ziyu Tian, Kaichen Shen, Wenbo Hao, Phillip Si, Peng Chen, Wei Zhu
bullets: Targets the computational cost of repeated full-state simulation and the limited coverage of sparse observations.
Uses a latent dynamics surrogate for ensemble forecast propagation.
Employs a VAE-based, state-dependent observation likelihood evaluated in latent space.
Applies a flow-matching ensemble filtering update to jointly infer latent states and uncertain parameters.
Outperforms a broad range of data assimilation methods across fluid, tsunami, and atmospheric benchmarks, according to the abstract.
